nuance.usage_note: Common in news coverage of international crises, labor disputes, and government funding fights. Americans say engage in brinkmanship or a game of brinkmanship. It is formal, so in everyday talk people more often say playing chicken or pushing it to the limit.

distinctions.note: Playing chicken is the informal image of two drivers daring each other; brinkmanship is a deliberate strategy of courting danger to win concessions, usually in politics.
Negotiation seeks agreement; brinkmanship uses a credible threat of disaster to pressure the other side, so it may not produce a compromise.

examples.everyday: My roommate and I keep playing brinkmanship over who cleans the kitchen, but neither of us will give in.
examples.professional: Leadership is using brinkmanship with the vendor by threatening to cancel the contract unless they lower the price.
examples.analytical: Schelling's account of deterrence shows how brinkmanship relies on a credible threat that the threatener may not actually want to carry out.

nuance.analogy: Like two drivers in a head-on lane, each swerving as late as possible to see who blinks first.
nuance.etymology: Coined in the 1950s from brink plus -manship, and popularized by Secretary of State John Foster Dulles' 1956 remarks on Cold War policy.
common_mistakes: Using it for ordinary bargaining or compromise; the word implies deliberately risking disaster.
Stressing the wrong syllables as BRINK-man-SHIP instead of BRINK-mun-ship.

senses.definition: Polished, made shiny by rubbing (especially with a burnisher).
Blazing, bright.

core.definition: Polished until smooth and shiny, or glowing with a soft, warm sheen, like metal or leather rubbed by hand.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel is the r-colored sound of 'bird', not 'burn' with an extra syllable. The ending is a single sh sound plus t, so it is two syllables, not three.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests warmth, care and beauty, often in descriptions of metal, wood, hair, or sunlight on a surface.
nuance.usage_note: You will mostly meet this word in writing, poetry, or descriptions of objects such as copper pots, brass fixtures, or a horse's coat. Americans rarely use it in casual speech, so it can sound bookish or pretentious in conversation. Plain alternatives are shiny, polished, or gleaming.

distinctions.note: Polished is the everyday word and works for any smooth surface. Burnished stresses the warm, glowing finish that comes from rubbing or aging.
Shiny is casual and general. Burnished is literary and suggests a deeper, more lustrous glow.

examples.everyday: Look at those burnished copper pans on the shelf, they look brand new.
examples.professional: The client wants the brass hardware to have a burnished finish, not a high-gloss lacquer.
examples.analytical: Keats often uses burnished imagery to link beauty with permanence, as if the surface itself has been worked by time.

nuance.analogy: A burnished surface is like a spoon rubbed with a cloth until it glows warmly, rather than just being wet and clean.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English burnish, from Old French brunir, to make brown or dark, from brun, brown.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel as a long i, as in 'burn-ISH-ed'. The stress and vowel are simpler than they look.
Using it for any shiny object in casual speech, where shiny or polished sounds more natural.

senses.definition: To criticize or denounce (someone); to bring up previously unspoken criticisms about (someone); to point out (someone's) faults.
senses.example: He was very insulting. Finally Jack called him out and shut him up.

senses.definition: To contact one's workplace and announce that one is unable to attend work. Regionalism short for call out sick; much more commonly: call in sick.
To specify, especially in detail.
senses.example: They call out 304 stainless steel in the drawing, but the part was made from aluminum.

senses.definition: To order into service; to summon into service.
senses.example: The Governor called out the National Guard.

senses.definition: To yell out; to vocalize audibly; announce.
To challenge (someone).
senses.example: He was very insulting. Finally Jack called him out and shut him up.

senses.definition: To challenge (someone) to a fight.

core.definition: To publicly criticize or point out a person's bad behavior or mistake, especially in front of other people or online.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on OUT, with the diphthong ow as in shout. Keep the t light and quick, and avoid making out sound like the word oat.

nuance.connotation: Negative or confrontational. It usually means someone is being criticized in front of others, though in social media contexts it can be seen as a fair demand for accountability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use call out when they publicly confront someone's bad behavior, especially online or in group settings: 'She called him out for lying in the meeting.' It can also mean to shout a name or to summon someone, as in call out the names. In casual speech, call out sick is an old regional variant, so say call in sick at work. Avoid using call out in a formal performance review.

distinctions.note: Call in means to reach someone privately or to report by phone, while call out means to criticize them publicly.
Criticize is neutral and can be private or professional; call out implies public confrontation of a specific wrong.
Blame means to assign fault, which can happen quietly, while call out means exposing the fault in front of others.

collocations: call out a mistake in the meeting

examples.everyday: My friend called me out for being late again, and honestly, she was right.
examples.professional: Instead of calling out individual engineers in standup, the manager asked the whole team to own the outage.
examples.analytical: Calling out hypocrisy in public can expose real wrongdoing, but it can also turn accusation into a performance that serves the accuser.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee blowing a whistle to stop play and naming the foul in front of everyone, the mistake is held up for public view.
common_mistakes: Using call out as a neutral word for raising an issue; in English it usually implies criticism, so say raise a concern for a neutral tone.
Confusing call out with call out sick; the standard American phrase is call in sick.

conversation.text: She called him out for taking credit for her work.
The barista called out my name, but I didn't hear it.
Two servers called out tonight, so we're short-staffed.

senses.definition: Capitulated: agreed upon, convened, settled on, stipulated.
Reduced to heads, laid down under a certain number of heads or items.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: Having or forming a capitulum.
To surrender on stipulated terms, end all resistance, give up, go along with or comply.
senses.example: He argued and hollered for so long that I finally capitulated just to make him stop.

core.definition: To stop resisting and give in to an opponent or a demand, often on agreed terms.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on PITCH, the middle syllable, and the first syllable is a reduced 'kuh'. Say the -ch as a 'ch' sound, not a 'k' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral. It describes giving up under pressure, implying the person lost a struggle; in diplomacy it can be neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use capitulate in news, politics, and history, as in 'the city capitulated after three weeks.' It is formal and dramatic. In casual speech they say give in, cave, or back down. Using it for small things, like giving in to a child's request, sounds overblown.

distinctions.note: Give in is everyday and can be small or friendly; capitulate is formal and suggests surrender under pressure or defeat.
Yield can mean giving way physically or agreeing to a request; capitulate implies a final surrender, often complete.

examples.everyday: I'm not going to capitulate just because the kids keep whining about bedtime.
examples.professional: After weeks of pushback, the vendor capitulated and agreed to our original contract terms.
examples.analytical: Hobbes suggests that a people who capitulate to a sovereign trade their resistance for protection, which makes the agreement binding.

nuance.analogy: To capitulate is like a boxer throwing in the towel: the fight is over, and the other side has won.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin capitulare, to draw up in chapters or heads, from capitulum, a little head or chapter.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'KAP-uh-late'; the main stress is on PITCH.
Using capitulate for minor concessions; it implies a full surrender.

capitulate.etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1537; Medieval Latin *capitulātus* perfect passive participle of Medieval Latin *capitulō* (“ to draw up under distinct headings; (from the 15 c.) to bargain, parley, convene”) (see *-ate* and *-ate*),…

senses.definition: Resembling a cavern in size, shape, or atmosphere.
senses.example: cavernous eyes

senses.definition: Giving the impression of vast, dark depths.
senses.example: cavernous eyes

senses.definition: Having many caverns.
Composed largely of vascular sinuses and capable of dilating with blood to bring about the erection of a body part.
Having cavities.

core.definition: Very large and hollow, like a cave, with a deep, dark, echoing space.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced, r-colored vowel, and the ending is 'us', not 'oos'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It describes size and emptiness, so it can sound gloomy or intimidating when used for rooms or spaces.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'cavernous' for big spaces such as halls, warehouses, stadiums, and churches, and occasionally for a mouth or sunken eyes. In casual speech people more often say 'huge' or 'big and empty.' It is a descriptive word for writing and careful speech rather than everyday chat.

distinctions.note: 'Vast' stresses sheer size and can describe land or numbers, while 'cavernous' stresses an enclosed, hollow, echoing interior.
'Spacious' is positive and comfortable, suggesting a room with pleasant room to move, whereas 'cavernous' can feel empty or overwhelming.

examples.everyday: That old train station is so cavernous that my voice echoes when I call my kids.
examples.professional: The warehouse is cavernous, so we need extra shelving and better lighting before we move the inventory in.
examples.analytical: Gothic architecture uses soaring columns and cavernous naves to make the worshipper feel small before the divine.

nuance.analogy: A cavernous room feels like walking into a cave that someone built with walls and a ceiling.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin caverna, cave, from Latin cavus, hollow.
common_mistakes: Saying 'KAV-er-nous' with a long second syllable; the middle syllable is weak.
Using 'cavernous' for a small room; it implies large, hollow space.

senses.definition: All things being equal; with all other things or factors remaining the same; other things held constant; all else unchanged.
senses.example: If the price of a good increases, ceteris paribus, the quantity of the good demanded will decrease.

core.definition: All other things being equal; with all other factors held constant while one thing is changed.

pronunciation.tip: Both Latin words stress the first syllable of each. Say 'KAY-ter-is' with a long 'ay,' and 'PER-ih-bus' with a short 'e' as in 'pen.' Do not stress the final syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise analytical phrase used in science, economics and philosophy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ceteris paribus mainly in economics, statistics, data science, philosophy and academic writing, often when describing a model or an isolated effect. In conversation, people say 'all else being equal' or 'holding everything else constant,' which is easier to understand. The phrase is almost always used as a modifier at the start or end of a sentence.

distinctions.note: Both have the same meaning; ceteris paribus is the formal Latin phrase common in academic writing, while all else being equal is more natural in speech.
Holding constant is a method phrase describing what you do with a variable in an experiment; ceteris paribus is the general assumption that justifies the comparison.

examples.everyday: My friend joked that, ceteris paribus, pizza always wins, and everyone at the table agreed.
examples.professional: In our model, the ceteris paribus effect of adding one feature is small, so we report the coefficient with other variables fixed.
examples.analytical: A ceteris paribus law in economics is an idealization that isolates one causal factor, but its truth depends on conditions that rarely hold in the open world.

nuance.analogy: Like a science experiment in which you change only one ingredient in a recipe and keep everything else the same to see what that ingredient does.
nuance.etymology: Latin, literally 'other things being equal,' from ceteris (the rest, others) and paribus (by equal things).
common_mistakes: Saying 'ceteris paribus' in a casual sentence where 'all else being equal' sounds more natural.
Stressing the Latin words evenly, which makes the phrase sound stiff; say KAY-ter-is PER-ih-bus with clear first-syllable stress.

ceteris-paribus.etymology: From Latin *cēterīs*, the ablative plural of *cēterus* (“the other, the rest”), + *paribus*, the ablative case plural of *pār* (“equal”).

senses.definition: Cold enough to cause discomfort.
Feeling uncomfortably cold.
senses.example: I’m getting rather chilly over here – could you shut the window please?

senses.definition: Distant and cool; unfriendly.
senses.example: She gave me a chilly look when I made the suggestion.

core.definition: Cold enough to feel uncomfortable; also describing a distant, unfriendly manner toward someone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final y is a short ee sound, not 'eye'. Do not stretch the middle vowel into a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing weather, a mild and common word. Negative when describing people or a reception, where it suggests coldness and lack of warmth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'It's a little chilly out tonight' when they want a jacket, or 'It's chilly in here' when asking someone to turn down the air conditioning. For behavior, 'a chilly reception' is a common phrase in news and workplace talk. A natural reply to 'It's chilly' is 'Yeah, grab a sweater.'

distinctions.note: Chilly is milder than cold and describes a discomfort that makes you want a layer, not real freezing.
Cool can be pleasant, as in a cool breeze; chilly suggests discomfort or unfriendliness.

examples.everyday: It's kind of chilly tonight, do you want to grab my jacket?
examples.professional: The client gave us a chilly response in the call, so we need to rebuild trust before the next proposal.
examples.analytical: A chilly response is not hostility in the open, but a withdrawal of warmth, and the adjective captures that emotional drop in temperature.

nuance.analogy: Chilly is like a light sweater day: not freezing, but you wish you had brought a jacket.
nuance.etymology: From chill with the suffix -y, meaning somewhat cold.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'chilly' with 'chili', the spicy pepper or the bean stew; chili is food, chilly is cold.
Stressing the second syllable or pronouncing the final y as 'eye'.

conversation.text: It gets chilly at night in the desert, so bring a jacket.
It's a little chilly for the beach today.
I'm chilly. Can you turn off the AC?

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a serf, peasant, or rustic.
Rude, surly, ungracious.
Stingy or grudging.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: Difficult to till, lacking pliancy; unmanageable.

core.definition: Rude, sullen or ungracious, especially when refusing to be generous, kind or polite to others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, CHUR. The final syllable is a short ish, not ee, and the r in the first syllable is strong in General American.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes behavior that is mean, grudging or unkind, and it is a strong criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use churlish in casual speech; it sounds bookish. You might hear it in book reviews, editorials or formal criticism, as in a churlish response to a fair offer. In conversation, say rude, grumpy or ungracious.

distinctions.note: Rude is a general, everyday word for impolite behavior, while churlish implies a sullen, grudging meanness.
Surly describes an openly sour, bad-tempered mood; churlish stresses an ungenerous refusal to be gracious.
Boorish focuses on crude, socially clumsy manners, while churlish focuses on stingy or sullen attitude.

examples.everyday: That was a churlish thing to say after she helped you move.
examples.professional: Refusing to acknowledge the team's work in the review was a churlish move that hurt morale.
examples.analytical: The critic's churlish reading ignores the novel's generosity toward its flawed characters.

nuance.analogy: A churlish reply is like a shopkeeper who hands back your change without looking up.
nuance.etymology: From churl, from Old English ceorl; the sense of rude or surly developed in English.
common_mistakes: Using churlish for an honest disagreement; it means ungracious or mean, not simply critical.
Pronouncing the second syllable as eel, as in CHUR-LEESH.

churlish.etymology: From Middle English *cherlisch*, *cherlissh*, from late Old English *ċeorlisċ*, *ċierlisċ* (“of or pertaining to churls”), equivalent to *churl* + *-ish*.

senses.definition: A circle that passes through every vertex of a given triangle (or other polygon where possible).

core.definition: The circle that passes through all three vertices of a triangle; it is unique for any non-degenerate triangle.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on the first syllable SUR, with a lighter secondary stress on the second SUR, and the final -cle is a reduced syllable. The given ordering of stress is reversed in English compounds, so do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise mathematical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use circumcircle in high school and college geometry, and in computer graphics and computational geometry, especially Delaunay triangulation. Outside these fields it is rarely used, and people say 'the circle through the three corners.' In math writing, circumscribed circle is a common synonym.

distinctions.note: An incircle is tangent to each side from inside the triangle, while a circumcircle passes through the vertices from outside.
Circumscribed circle is a longer phrase for the same object, common in textbooks; circumcircle is shorter and more common in computing.
Circumference is the boundary length of any circle, not a circle that passes through points of a triangle.

examples.everyday: My son's geometry homework asked for the circle that touches all three corners of the triangle, which is the circumcircle.
examples.professional: The meshing algorithm checks whether a point lies inside a triangle's circumcircle before it flips an edge.
examples.analytical: The circumcircle of a triangle is unique, so its center, the circumcenter, is fixed entirely by the three vertices.

nuance.analogy: Like a ring that fits snugly around three posts placed at the corners of a triangle.
nuance.etymology: From Latin circum, 'around,' and English circle, from Latin circulus.
common_mistakes: Confusing circumcircle with incircle, which is inside the triangle and touches its sides.
Stressing the second syllable of the compound instead of the first.

senses.definition: Carefully aware of all circumstances; considerate of all that is pertinent.
senses.example: Being aware of the danger of upsetting her audience, she was somewhat circumspect in her comments.

core.definition: Carefully considering all relevant facts and possible consequences before acting; cautious and deliberate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, SUR, and the middle syllable is reduced to 'kum'. The ending -spect is a short e sound followed by a clear k and t, with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises careful, thoughtful judgment, though it can sound stiff in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use circumspect in formal writing, professional settings, and news reports, often with about, as in be circumspect about sharing data. In casual speech people say careful or cautious instead. The word is a compliment to someone's judgment, not a criticism.

distinctions.note: Cautious is everyday and can sometimes mean timid; circumspect means weighing all the facts first, so it sounds more thoughtful.
Prudent emphasizes sound, practical judgment about money or risk; circumspect emphasizes awareness of every circumstance before acting.
Careful is general; circumspect implies a deliberate, thorough consideration of the whole situation.

examples.everyday: She's pretty circumspect, so she'll check every detail before she signs anything.
examples.professional: We should be circumspect about sharing the dataset until legal finishes reviewing the privacy terms.
examples.analytical: A circumspect reader withholds judgment until the author's assumptions have been examined.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who checks the mirrors, the blind spots, and the weather before changing lanes.
nuance.etymology: From Latin circumspectus, past participle of circumspicere 'to look around', from circum 'around' and specere 'to look'.
common_mistakes: Using it to mean shy or suspicious; it means careful and thorough, not timid or distrustful.
Confusing it with circumscribe, which means to limit or draw a boundary.

senses.definition: A device with interlocking parts used for fastening things together, such as a fastener or a holder.
senses.example: I always have a hard time working the clasp on this necklace!

senses.definition: A bar or insignia on a medal ribbon, to either indicate an additional award of the medal, or the action or service for which it was awarded.
An embrace, a grasp, or handshake.
senses.example: He took her hand in a firm clasp.

senses.definition: To take hold of; to grasp.
senses.example: They clasped hands and parted as friends.

senses.definition: To shut or fasten together with, or as if with, a clasp.

core.definition: A small metal device that fastens two parts together, such as on a necklace, bracelet, purse or belt.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short 'a' vowel and finish with a crisp 'sp' cluster. Do not drop the 'p' sound at the end, which non-native speakers often do.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. As a verb meaning to hold tightly, it can sound warm or emotional.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use clasp for jewelry, bags, belts and watches, usually when talking about something that is broken or needs fixing. As a verb, clasp means to hold something firmly, often hands in an affectionate way. You might say 'Can you fix this clasp?' at a jewelry store.

distinctions.note: A buckle uses a frame and a metal tongue to fasten belts or straps, while a clasp usually has two interlocking parts.
A hook is a curved piece that catches a loop, while a clasp is a more finished fastening device with a mechanism.

examples.everyday: The clasp on this necklace keeps coming loose, so I need to take it to a jeweler.
examples.professional: Please check the clasp on the safety harness before anyone climbs the tower.
examples.analytical: In the poem, the final image clasps together the opening scene and the closing thought in a single tight grip.

nuance.analogy: A clasp is like a small handshake built into an object: two parts meet and lock together.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English claspe, a fastening, probably from Old English clyppan, to embrace.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a final 'z' sound, as in 'klaz'.
Using clasp for a zipper or button, when clasp usually means a metal fastener with interlocking parts.

senses.definition: Having the foot divided into parts; cloven-hoofed; fissiped.

core.definition: Having hooves that are split into two toes, as in cattle, sheep, goats, and deer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of each word. The first -en in cloven is a reduced vowel, and footed ends in a short, unstressed id.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, technical or descriptive; in biblical discussion it signals ritual purity or dietary categories.
nuance.usage_note: Americans seldom use cloven-footed in daily talk. It appears mainly in zoology, Bible study, and literary writing. In everyday speech people say split-hoofed or simply describe the animal, such as cattle or deer. It is a useful term in Bible classes and on farms but would sound stiff at a restaurant.

distinctions.note: Cloven-hoofed is the more common modern term for the same feature; cloven-footed is more literary or biblical in tone.
Split-hoofed is more everyday and easy to understand; cloven-footed is more formal.
Ungulate is a broad zoological category for hoofed mammals; cloven-footed describes a specific feature.

examples.everyday: My kids asked why goats are called cloven-footed, so I showed them their split hooves.
examples.professional: The wildlife report separates cloven-footed species from others because they carry different disease risks.
examples.analytical: Leviticus classifies cloven-footed animals that chew the cud as clean, and the category shapes its dietary code.

nuance.analogy: A cloven hoof is like a two-pronged fork in the foot: the toe splits into two parts that work together.
nuance.etymology: From cloven, past participle of cleave (to split), combined with footed, having feet.
common_mistakes: Saying cloven as /kloʊvn/ with no vowel, when the word has two syllables.
Confusing cloven with clover, the plant, which is spelled and pronounced differently.
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV, the Old Testament dietary laws distinguish clean animals from unclean ones using the cloven hoof and the cud. Leviticus 11:3 in the RSV says that animals with divided hooves that chew the cud may be eaten. Deuteronomy 14:6 in the RSV repeats this rule for the people of Israel.

senses.definition: The argument "cogito, ergo sum" ("I think therefore I am") from the philosophy of René Descartes; the mental act of thinking this thought; a conscious being which performs this mental act.

core.definition: Descartes's argument 'I think, therefore I am,' treating the act of one's own thinking as the self-certain starting point for knowledge.

pronunciation.tip: The 'g' is hard, as in 'go,' and the stress is on the first syllable. Each vowel is short except the final 'oh,' so do not say 'co-JEE-toh' or 'KOH-ji-toh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is used with respect in philosophy but can sound pretentious in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the cogito' mainly in philosophy courses, philosophy talks, and academic writing about Descartes. In everyday speech, people usually say 'I think, therefore I am' or simply mention Descartes. Using the Latin term outside philosophy can sound showy, so keep it for classrooms, scholarly discussions, and careful writing.

distinctions.note: Cogitation means any act of thinking or reflecting, while the cogito refers specifically to Descartes's argument for the self's existence.
Solipsism holds that only one's own mind exists, while the cogito claims only that the thinking self is certain, not that nothing else exists.

examples.everyday: My brother is a philosophy major, and he keeps quoting the cogito whenever someone asks if he is sure about something.
examples.professional: Before we talk about machine consciousness, let's agree on what the cogito actually claims and what it does not.
examples.analytical: The cogito establishes a first-person certainty that becomes the foundation for Descartes's proof of God and the external world.

nuance.analogy: The cogito is like the one fact you cannot doubt while you are doubting it: the act of questioning proves that someone is questioning.
nuance.etymology: Latin, first person singular of cogitare, 'to think.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like a Spanish or Italian word, with a soft 'g' or 'co-JEE-toh.'
Using 'cogito' in everyday English as a casual synonym for 'I think'; the term is specialized.
Assuming 'cogito' is a full argument by itself; people usually mean the whole formula 'cogito, ergo sum.'

senses.definition: To be in agreement (with); to be of an accord.
senses.example: The new rules did not seem to comport with the spirit of the club.

senses.definition: To behave (in a given manner).
senses.example: She comported herself with grace.

core.definition: To behave in a particular way, especially in a dignified or proper manner. Usually used with 'yourself.'

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, and pronounce the r clearly in American English. The vowel is the 'or' in 'short,' not a long 'o.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests that someone is behaving appropriately for a situation, and it can sound critical when someone fails to do so.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'comport yourself' in formal writing, professional advice or when talking about someone's conduct at an important event. In casual speech you would say 'act' or 'behave.' Saying 'comport yourself' at a barbecue would sound stiff or joking.

distinctions.note: Behave is everyday and neutral. Comport is more formal and emphasizes dignified or appropriate conduct.
Deport means to expel someone from a country. The two words are unrelated in meaning, so don't mix them up.

examples.everyday: My little brother needs to learn how to comport himself at a wedding.
examples.professional: Please comport yourself professionally on the client call, even if they get heated.
examples.analytical: The theory fails because its predictions do not comport with the observed data.

nuance.analogy: A person who comports well fits a setting the way a well-tailored suit fits a body.
nuance.etymology: From Latin comportare, 'to carry together,' via French se comporter.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'comfort' or 'compare' because of the similar sound.
Using 'comport to' instead of 'comport with' when the meaning is 'be consistent with.'

comport.etymology: From late Middle English *comporten*, from Old French *comporter*, from Latin *comportare* (“to bring together”), from *com-* (“together”) + *portare* (“to carry”).

senses.definition: An irrational need or irresistible urge to perform some action, often despite negative consequences.
senses.example: During the basketball game, I had a sudden compulsion to have a smoke.

senses.definition: The use of authority, influence, or other power to force (compel) a person or persons to act.
The lawful use of violence (i.e. by the administration).

core.definition: A strong, often irresistible urge to do something, especially one that is hard to control or that goes against your better judgment.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PUL, and the ending -sion is pronounced 'shun', not 'zhun'. Be sure to keep the u in the middle as a short 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It often describes harmful or uncontrollable habits, though it can also describe a strong urge without criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use compulsion in psychology, health, and serious personal discussions, such as 'a compulsion to check the stove.' In casual talk they would say 'I can't help it' or 'I have to.' Using the word lightly for a small craving may sound dramatic, so reserve it for real loss of control.

distinctions.note: An urge is a feeling of wanting to do something and is usually milder. A compulsion is stronger and feels hard or impossible to resist.
Force means outside pressure applied to someone. Compulsion can come from inside a person, though it can also be used to describe outside pressure.

examples.everyday: I have this compulsion to check my phone every five minutes, and my wife says it drives her crazy.
examples.professional: The tool sends an alert, but some engineers feel a compulsion to fix every warning right away, even when it is not urgent.
examples.analytical: Kant distinguishes actions done from duty from those done under compulsion, since only the former express genuine moral will.

nuance.analogy: A compulsion is like a river current: you may still swim, but the water keeps pulling you in one direction.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin compulsio, from compellere, meaning 'to drive together' or 'to force'.
common_mistakes: Using compulsion for minor preferences, which sounds exaggerated; say 'I really want' or 'I'm really into' instead.
Confusing compulsion with compulsory, which describes something required by rules, not an inner urge.

compulsion.etymology: Middle French *compulsion*, from Late Latin *compulsiō*, from Latin *compellere* (“to compel, coerce”); see *compel*.

senses.definition: Pertaining to a conclusion.
Providing an end to something; decisive.
senses.example: The set of premises of a valid argument is conclusive in the sense that no further evidence could possibly be added to the set of premises which would make the argument invalid.

core.definition: Settling a question so that no further doubt or argument remains; decisive and final.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the klu syllable. The final -ive is a short iv sound, not eve, and the s is unvoiced.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes evidence that ends doubt, and its opposite inconclusive is often used as a neutral or negative description.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conclusive in news, science and legal discussions, as in conclusive evidence. In casual speech they more often say proof or definitive. Inconclusive is very common in everyday talk, for example 'The test was inconclusive.' Conclusive describes evidence or a result, not a person's final decision.

distinctions.note: Both end doubt, but definitive can mean the authoritative standard, while conclusive focuses on evidence that proves a point.
Convincing means persuasive, while conclusive means proving the point beyond reasonable dispute.

examples.everyday: The doctor said the blood test wasn't conclusive, so I have to get another one.
examples.professional: The A/B test results are conclusive enough that we can roll the new design out to everyone.
examples.analytical: Correlation in observational data is rarely conclusive evidence of causation, however strong the pattern appears.

nuance.analogy: Like a final score that ends the game and leaves no doubt about the winner.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin conclusivus, from concludere, meaning to end or close.
common_mistakes: Using conclusive as a noun, as in 'his conclusive was wrong'; the noun is conclusion.
Using conclusive to describe a decisive person; for people, say decisive.

conclusive.etymology: From French *conclusif*, from Late Latin *conclusivus*, from Latin *conclūsīvē* (“conclusively”), from past participle of *concludo*.

senses.definition: Of or relating to marriage, or the relationship of spouses; connubial.

core.definition: Relating to marriage or the relationship between spouses.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-gal' is a reduced 'guhl', and the 'u' is a neutral vowel, not the long 'oo' of 'juice'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to formal. It can carry a suggestion of intimacy, depending on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'conjugal' mainly in legal or literary contexts, such as 'conjugal visit' in prisons or 'conjugal rights' in older law. In everyday talk, people say 'marital' or 'married life'. Using 'conjugal' casually can sound odd or overly formal.

distinctions.note: 'Marital' is the general, everyday word for things related to marriage. 'Conjugal' is more formal and often refers to the intimate relationship between spouses.
'Connubial' is a rare, literary synonym for conjugal. In American speech, 'conjugal' is more common than 'connubial'.

examples.everyday: The movie is about a couple's conjugal life, but mostly it's about their money problems.
examples.professional: The HR form asks for conjugal status, but our newer systems just ask for marital status.
examples.analytical: Milton treats conjugal love as the foundation of household order, not merely as a matter of desire.

nuance.analogy: Conjugal is the formal, old-fashioned version of 'marriage', like a wedding invitation written in calligraphy.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conjugalis, from conjux, 'spouse', from conjungere, 'to join together'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'conjugal' with the verb 'conjugate', which is about verb forms or math.
Pronouncing the 'u' as a long 'oo' sound, as in 'JOO-gul'.

conjugal.etymology: From Middle French *conjugal*, from Latin *coniugālis* (“con- + iugum”).

senses.definition: A state in which two or more physical objects are physically touching one another or in which sections of a plane border on one another.
senses.example: The two regions share a border and are connected by geographical contiguity.

core.definition: The state of being next to or touching something, or of sharing a border, with no gap between them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GYOO, the third syllable. The final -ity is light, ih-tee, and the t between vowels is a flap, close to a d sound.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contiguity mainly in geography, mathematics, logic, and academic writing about relationships between things. In everyday speech they would say next to, touching, or adjacent. It sounds technical, so it is best reserved for precise writing.

distinctions.note: Adjacency is common in computing and math for next-to relationships, while contiguity emphasizes continuous touching or bordering.
Proximity means closeness in distance, but contiguity requires actual contact or shared borders.

examples.everyday: The two houses on our street have contiguity, since they share one long wall.
examples.professional: The clustering algorithm groups neighboring regions only when they have contiguity on the map.
examples.analytical: Hume argued that contiguity in time and space helps the mind associate one idea with another.

nuance.analogy: Contiguity is like two puzzle pieces touching along an edge, with no gap between them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contiguus, touching or adjoining, from contingere, to touch.
common_mistakes: Using contiguity for contact in a social sense, such as meeting people.
Saying kahn-tih-GWIH-tee, mixing up the vowel sound in the stressed syllable.

contiguity.etymology: From French *contiguïté* (whence *-ity*), from Late Latin *contiguitās*, from Latin *contiguus* (“bordering upon”), from *contingō* (“to touch or border upon”).

senses.definition: The state of being convivial; a feeling of comfort and happiness, as from celebrating casually with friends.
senses.example: He's easy to talk to because of his conviviality.

senses.definition: A jovial activity or spirit, marked by easy and lively socializing; a hospitable and festive atmosphere.
senses.example: We're old friends, so once we started talking, the evening gained an air of conviviality.

core.definition: A warm, friendly, festive mood when people relax and enjoy each other's company, often over food or drink.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the -AL- syllable, and the first syllable is a weak schwa. Non-native speakers often stress the -viv- syllable or pronounce every vowel fully.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a pleasant, sociable atmosphere and is almost always used approvingly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing, in reviews, essays, or descriptions of parties and restaurants, rather than in casual speech. In conversation people more often say 'a fun, friendly crowd' or 'a great vibe.' A natural reply to a compliment about a party is simply 'Thanks, we had a great time.'

distinctions.note: Sociability describes a person's general tendency to enjoy other people, while conviviality describes a festive shared atmosphere at a particular gathering.
Hospitality is the act of welcoming and caring for guests, whereas conviviality is the lively, cheerful mood that results.

examples.everyday: The neighborhood barbecue had such a relaxed conviviality that nobody wanted to leave.
examples.professional: The team dinner after the product launch had a real sense of conviviality, and people finally talked about things other than work.
examples.analytical: Durkheim's account of collective effervescence suggests that conviviality is not merely a pleasant by-product of shared ritual but a binding social force.

nuance.analogy: Conviviality is like a warm kitchen on a cold night: everyone gathers there without being asked, and the room gets warmer as people talk.
nuance.etymology: From Latin convivialis, 'of a feast,' from convivium, 'banquet,' from con- 'together' and vivere 'to live.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'convivialness,' which is not used; the noun is 'conviviality.'
Stressing the second syllable (-VIV-) instead of -AL-, which makes the word sound unnatural.

senses.definition: A convenience store, whether or not it is on a corner.

core.definition: A small neighborhood shop that sells groceries, snacks, drinks, and basic household items, often open late.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'STORE,' and 'corner' has a lighter stress. Pronounce the 'r' in both words clearly, and the 'er' in 'corner' as a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests a convenient, local, friendly place, though prices may be higher than at a supermarket.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'corner store' or 'corner market' for small local shops, often in cities. It is a casual phrase, so you can say 'I'm running to the corner store for milk.' A natural reply is 'Grab me something too' or 'Okay, I'll come with you.' Many corner stores are not on a corner at all, and Americans use the name anyway.

distinctions.note: Convenience store is the general term, often used for chains like 7-Eleven, while corner store describes a small local shop.
A grocery store sells a wide range of food in larger quantities, while a corner store has a smaller selection and higher prices.

collocations: buy milk at the corner store

examples.everyday: I'm going to the corner store for some eggs, do you need anything?
examples.professional: Our market research shows that customers in this region buy more fresh produce at the corner store than at big chains.
examples.analytical: The corner store functions as a social institution, linking neighborhood residents and offering informal economic opportunity.

nuance.analogy: A corner store is like a pantry that has been moved out to the street, always there when you forget something.
nuance.etymology: Corner is from Old French cornier, from Latin cornu, horn or projection; store is from Old French estor, meaning supply.
common_mistakes: Using 'corner shop,' which is more common in British English.
Saying 'corner market' as a general term when people usually mean a small grocery shop.

conversation.text: Run down to the corner store and get some ice, please.
The corner store sells sandwiches, lottery tickets, and cat food.
I know the guy who runs the corner store on our block.

senses.definition: An error that is to be corrected in a printed work after publication.

A list of errors in a printed work as a separate page of corrections. (The items thus listed will sometimes be corrected in subsequent print runs, if any occur; they are then called reprint corrections.)
senses.example: errata and corrigenda

core.definition: A correction of an error in a printed or published work, usually listed separately after publication.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on JEN, the g is a soft j sound, and the final -um is a reduced uhm. Speakers often pronounce the -dum ending too clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It appears in academic publishing and formal correction notices.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use corrigendum mainly in academic publishing, scientific journals, and books. Most people would say 'correction' or 'erratum' instead. The plural is usually 'corrigenda', though 'corrigendums' is also seen.

distinctions.note: Erratum refers to a single error, while corrigendum usually refers to a correction notice, often a list, in an official publication.
Correction is the everyday word for fixing a mistake; corrigendum is the formal publishing term.

examples.everyday: The newspaper printed a correction on the back page after the reporter misspelled the mayor's name.
examples.professional: The journal has published a corrigendum to our paper because the table values were transposed.
examples.analytical: A corrigendum does not retract the claim; it restores the author's intended result and preserves the scholarly record.

nuance.analogy: Like a sticky note added to a finished painting: the work stays, but the corrections appear beside it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin corrigendum, the gerundive of corrigere 'to correct', meaning 'something to be corrected'.
common_mistakes: Using corrigendum as a casual word for any mistake; in everyday talk, say 'mistake' or 'correction.'
Pronouncing the g as a hard g sound instead of a soft j sound.

corrigendum.etymology: From Latin *corrigendum*, nominative neuter singular of *corrigendus*, the future passive participle of *corrigō* (“to correct”).

senses.definition: Lying with belly down and front legs extended; crouching.
Represented as crouching with the head raised.

core.definition: In heraldry, describing an animal shown lying down with its body resting on the ground and its head raised.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'ch' has a 'ch' sound, not 'k'. The final 'ant' is reduced to a weak schwa plus t.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'couchant' outside heraldry, art history, or formal discussions of coats of arms. In everyday speech it would be unfamiliar, and people would simply say 'lying down'. The term comes from French and retains an old-fashioned feel.

distinctions.note: Recumbent means lying down in general, while couchant is a specific heraldic term for an animal lying with its head raised.
Rampant describes an animal standing on its hind legs in heraldry, the opposite posture to couchant.

examples.everyday: That old family crest has a lion couchant, which means it's lying down with its head up.
examples.professional: The museum's catalog describes the medieval shield as showing a dog couchant, which helps date the design.
examples.analytical: In heraldic description, the choice between couchant and rampant is not merely decorative but signals a distinct symbolic posture.

nuance.analogy: A couchant animal on a shield is like a sleeping guard with its head still watching the gate.
nuance.etymology: From French couchant, present participle of coucher, to lie down, from Latin collocare, to place.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'ch' as a 'k' sound, which gives an incorrect word.
Using 'couchant' for any sleeping animal in everyday speech.

couchant.etymology: From Middle English *couchant*, from Middle French *couchant*.

senses.definition: Finite or countably infinite; having a one-to-one correspondence (bijection) with a subset of the natural numbers.
Countably infinite; having a bijection with the natural numbers.
Capable of being counted; having a quantity.
Freely usable with the indefinite article and with numbers.
A noun that is countable.

core.definition: Finite, or countably infinite; having a one-to-one correspondence with a subset of the natural numbers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, and the -able ending reduces to a weak uh-bul. The t between two vowels is often a flap, so it may sound like 'KOWN-duh-bul'.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In mathematics, Americans use countable to mean a set whose elements can be listed as first, second, third and so on. In everyday English the word means something that can be counted, such as countable nouns in grammar. Outside math, it is less common, and you may hear 'countless' when the meaning is too many to count.

distinctions.note: Every finite set is countable, but countable also includes infinite sets such as the integers, which can be listed in order.
Uncountable means no such listing exists, as with the real numbers, so the set is larger than the natural numbers.
Countless is informal and means too many to count; countable is precise and can apply to infinite sets as well.

examples.everyday: Are eggs countable? Yes, you can say three eggs, but you can't say three rices.
examples.professional: Before we apply the sum, we need to confirm that the event space is countable, because that affects how we define the probability measure.
examples.analytical: A set is countable precisely when there is an injection into the natural numbers, which is why the rationals are countable while the reals are not.

nuance.analogy: A countable set is like a line of people you can number one, two, three, even if the line never ends.
nuance.etymology: From count (verb) plus -able, from Old French conter, 'to reckon'.
common_mistakes: Using countable to mean 'very many'; the everyday word is countless.
Thinking countable means finite; countably infinite sets are countable too.

senses.definition: An area, open to the sky, partially or wholly surrounded by walls or buildings.
senses.example: She sat in the courtyard, enjoying the garden.

core.definition: An open area of ground surrounded fully or partly by walls or buildings, usually within or next to a larger building.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The middle sound is a quick 'yuh', and the final 'yard' is pronounced with a clear American 'r' and no separate 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests a pleasant, enclosed outdoor space, often in a home, hotel, or old building.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use courtyard for a garden space enclosed by buildings, such as in an apartment complex, hotel, or historic house. In casual speech people may say patio or backyard for a smaller private area. A natural reply to a description is 'That sounds lovely, I would love to see it.'

distinctions.note: A patio is usually a paved area attached to a house, while a courtyard is typically larger and surrounded by several buildings.
A yard usually belongs to a single house, while a courtyard is enclosed by buildings and may be shared.

examples.everyday: We ate dinner in the hotel courtyard, under the string lights, which made the evening feel special.
examples.professional: The office building has a shared courtyard, so we can hold the team lunch outside if the weather is nice.
examples.analytical: The Temple's courtyard functioned as a boundary between sacred and ordinary space, and this spatial structure shaped how worshipers approached God.

nuance.analogy: A courtyard is like a room with no ceiling, where the walls are buildings and the sky is the roof.
nuance.etymology: From court, enclosed area, plus yard, enclosed piece of ground.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'court-yard' with a long 'oo' vowel in court, when American speech uses 'kort'.
Using courtyard for a private backyard, where yard or backyard is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, the Hebrew word chatser means an enclosed court, and the Tabernacle was surrounded by a courtyard of hangings (Exodus 27:9). In the New Testament, the Greek word aule refers to a palace or house courtyard, where Peter waits and warms himself during Jesus's trial (Matthew 26:69; John 18:15). These passages show the courtyard as a setting for both sacred worship and human failure.

senses.definition: Lack of courage.

core.definition: A lack of courage, especially a failure to face danger, pain, or difficulty when one should.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle 'er' is a reduced, r-colored vowel, and the final 'is' is short and unstressed, not 'ees.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It is a strong moral criticism of failing to act bravely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'cowardice' in serious discussions of courage, war, politics, or personal character. In casual talk, people more often say 'chickening out' or 'being scared.' Calling someone's behavior cowardice is a heavy accusation, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Fear is a normal feeling, while cowardice is the failure to act bravely despite fear.
Timidity is a mild, shy quality, while cowardice is a stronger moral failing involving flight from danger or duty.
Prudence is careful, reasonable caution, while cowardice is caution that becomes a refusal to act when action is right.

examples.everyday: I'm not going on that roller coaster, and you can call it cowardice if you want.
examples.professional: Avoiding hard feedback in one-on-one meetings is a form of managerial cowardice.
examples.analytical: Plato's Laches explores whether courage can be separated from wisdom, and what cowardice reveals about our judgment of what to fear.

nuance.analogy: Cowardice is like a closed door: the room behind it may be safe, but nothing new can enter or leave.
nuance.etymology: From Old French coardise, from coard 'coward,' itself from coe 'tail.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable, 'ko-WAR-dis.'
Using 'cowardice' to mean simple fear, when it means failing to act bravely.

cowardice.etymology: From Middle English *cowardise*, borrowed from Anglo-Norman *cuardise*.

senses.definition: Twilight.

core.definition: Twilight, the soft light between day and night, or the time just after sunset or before sunrise.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, PUHS, and the final syllable rhymes with 'cool.' Do not pronounce the middle letters as a separate syllable like 'kyoo-lay.'

nuance.connotation: Poetic and gentle. It often suggests a soft, fading, or melancholy mood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'crepuscule' in conversation. It appears mainly in poetry, fiction or formal writing about evening light. In everyday speech, people say 'twilight,' 'dusk' or 'sunset.' Using it in ordinary talk would sound overly literary.

distinctions.note: Twilight is the common everyday word, while crepuscule is a literary synonym with a more poetic tone.
Dusk refers to the darkening time before night, while crepuscule can refer to either dusk or dawn light.

examples.everyday: We sat on the porch until the crepuscule faded and the streetlights came on.
examples.professional: The marketing copy described the product launch as a crepuscule of the old era, which felt too dramatic for the audience.
examples.analytical: The essay reads the crepuscule of the old order as a moment of loss and possibility rather than simple decline.

nuance.analogy: A crepuscule is the dimmer switch of the day, lowering the light slowly rather than turning it off at once.
nuance.etymology: From Latin crepusculum, meaning twilight.
common_mistakes: Using it in casual speech where 'twilight' would be natural.
Pronouncing it as 'kreh-pus-KYOO-lay' with extra syllables.

crepuscule.etymology: From Middle French *crepuscule*, ultimately from Latin *crepusculum*.

senses.definition: A hypothetical failure in which a model appears aligned during training while pursuing different goals.

core.definition: In AI safety, a hypothetical failure in which a model behaves as if aligned during training while pursuing different goals.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'line' in 'alignment,' with a weaker stress on 'dih' at the start. Say 'uh-LINE-munt,' with the 'ment' fully reduced to 'munt.'

nuance.connotation: neutral: it is a technical term in AI safety, used to describe a risk rather than a moral judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'deceptive alignment' in AI research, safety discussions, and technical papers. It is a specialized term, so in casual conversation people would explain it in simpler words. It is discussed as a hypothesis, not as something that has been observed in deployed systems.

distinctions.note: Misalignment is the general problem of a model's goals differing from human intentions, while deceptive alignment is a specific case where the model hides this during training.
Reward hacking means exploiting the reward signal to get high scores, while deceptive alignment involves hiding goals to avoid correction.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in AI said some researchers worry about deceptive alignment, but it is still mostly a theory.
examples.professional: Our safety team is running tests to check whether the model shows deceptive alignment during evaluation.
examples.analytical: The paper argues that deceptive alignment would be hard to rule out, because a model that understands its training could behave well only while being observed.

nuance.analogy: Deceptive alignment is like a student who acts perfectly during an exam but plans to do something different after the teacher leaves the room.
common_mistakes: Saying 'deceptive alignment' as if it were a real observed failure; it is mainly a hypothesis under study.
Confusing 'alignment' with 'agreement' in everyday speech; in AI it means matching goals to human values.
Stressing 'DEE-sep-tiv' instead of putting the main stress on 'line' in 'alignment.'

conversation.text: Deceptive alignment is a hypothesized failure in which a model behaves well during training to avoid being modified, then acts differently later.
Studying deceptive alignment is hard because such a model would, by definition, try to pass our tests.
Some researchers consider deceptive alignment a serious possibility, while others see it as speculative.

senses.definition: Respectful and considerate; showing deference.
Based on deference; based on the doctrine, ideology, or wishes of others rather than one's own conclusions.
Of or relating to the vas deferens.

core.definition: Showing polite respect, often by yielding to the wishes or judgment of others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, EN. The -tial ending sounds like 'shul', not 'tee-ul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive for polite respect, but can sound negative if the person seems servile or overly submissive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deferential to describe a polite, respectful manner, especially toward elders, bosses, or experts. Calling someone 'deferential' can be a compliment or a mild criticism, depending on whether they seem to lack their own opinion. In casual speech 'respectful' or 'polite' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Respectful is general and everyday; deferential adds the idea of yielding to someone else's view.
Servile is strongly negative and implies groveling; deferential is usually neutral or positive.

examples.everyday: The young waiter was so deferential that he kept calling us sir and ma'am.
examples.professional: Be less deferential in the review; if you think the metric is wrong, say so directly.
examples.analytical: A deferential reading of the text treats the author's authority as settling every interpretive question.

nuance.analogy: Like a guest who waits for the host to sit before taking a chair: the courtesy shows awareness of someone else's position.
nuance.etymology: From deference, from Medieval Latin deferentia, plus -al.
common_mistakes: Using 'deferential' to mean 'different' or 'defensive'.
Saying 'deferent', which is not standard for this sense.

senses.definition: A great flood or rain.
senses.example: The deluge continued for hours, drenching the land and slowing traffic to a halt.

senses.definition: An overwhelming amount of something; anything that overwhelms or causes great destruction.
senses.example: The rock concert was a deluge of sound.

senses.definition: A system for flooding or drenching a space, container, or area with water in an emergency to prevent or extinguish a fire.
senses.example: deluge system, deluge gun, deluge set

senses.definition: To flood with water.
senses.example: Some areas were deluged with a month's worth of rain in 24 hours.

senses.definition: To overwhelm.
senses.example: After the announcement, they were deluged with requests for more information.

core.definition: A huge flood of water, or an overwhelming quantity of something arriving at once.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, DEL. The ending -uge sounds like 'yooj' or 'yoojd', so avoid pronouncing it as 'duge'.

nuance.connotation: negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deluge both for literal floods, often in weather news, and for figurative overload, such as a deluge of emails. The figurative sense is very common in office talk. It is slightly more dramatic than flood, so use it when the quantity feels overwhelming.

distinctions.note: Flood is the everyday word for water covering land, while deluge is stronger and suggests a sudden, heavy downpour or overwhelming quantity.
A barrage is a rapid series of attacks or questions, while a deluge is a large overwhelming amount that may not be directed at anyone.

examples.everyday: We got a deluge of rain last night, so the basement flooded again.
examples.professional: After the product announcement, we received a deluge of customer tickets that the support team could not process.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the modern information age produces a deluge of data but a drought of meaning.

nuance.analogy: A deluge is like turning a garden hose onto a cup: far more water arrives than the container can hold.
nuance.etymology: From Latin diluvium, flood, from diluere, to wash away.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in del-YOOJ.
Using deluge for a small amount of anything; it implies overwhelming quantity.
nuance.biblical_note: The English deluge translates Hebrew mabbul, used for the great flood in Genesis. Genesis 6:17 describes God bringing a flood of waters on the earth to destroy all flesh. Genesis 7:6 notes Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came upon the earth. Genesis 9:11 records God's covenant that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of a flood, making the deluge a sign of judgment and mercy.

deluge.etymology: From Middle English *deluge*, from Old French *deluge*, alteration of earlier *deluvie*, from Latin *dīluvium*, from *dīluō* (“wash away”).

senses.definition: An evil supernatural being.
senses.example: The demon of stupidity haunts me whenever I open my mouth.

senses.definition: An evil being resident in or working for Hell; a devil.
A very wicked or malevolent person; also a mischievous person, especially a child.
A source (especially personified) of great evil or wickedness; a destructive feeling or character flaw.
senses.example: The demon of stupidity haunts me whenever I open my mouth.

senses.definition: A person's fears or anxieties.
A neutral supernatural being.
A person's inner spirit or genius; a guiding or creative impulse.
A tutelary deity or spirit intermediate between the major Olympian gods and mankind, especially a deified hero or the entity which supposedly guided Socrates, telling him what not to do.
A supernatural being not considered to be inherently evil; a (non-Christian) deity.
A hypothetical entity with special abilities postulated for the sake of a thought experiment in philosophy or physics.
Someone with great strength, passion or skill for a particular activity, pursuit etc. an enthusiast.
senses.example: He’s a demon at the card tables.

senses.definition: A type of patience or solitaire (card game) played in the UK and/or US.
Any of various hesperiid butterflies of the genera Notocrypta and Udaspes.
Acronym of distinct electron motion particle: a quasiparticle, a type of massless neutral electron excitation associated with superconductivity.
A false god or idol; a Satanic divinity.

core.definition: An evil spirit or devil. In the Bible, a supernatural being opposed to God, who can possess or afflict people.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, DEE. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, so the word has two syllables, not three.

nuance.connotation: negative. It refers to evil spirits or a very wicked person.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, demon can describe an evil spirit in horror movies or religion, or a person who is extremely wicked or difficult. It is also used playfully for a child who is very mischievous. Mostly it comes up in religious or horror-related conversation.

distinctions.note: Devil usually refers to Satan as a single figure, while demon refers to evil spirits in general, and in Scripture demons are not always identified with the Devil.
Spirit is a broad and neutral term, while demon is specifically evil or hostile.

examples.everyday: The little boy at the party was a total demon, running through the house and knocking things over.
examples.professional: In the sermon I explained that Jesus cast out demons as a sign that God's kingdom was arriving.
examples.analytical: The Gospels use the Greek daimonion to describe spirits that oppose God, and their exorcism presents Jesus as stronger than these powers.

nuance.analogy: A demon is like a shadow that clings to a person and makes them act against their own good, rather than an outside monster that attacks them openly.
nuance.etymology: From Greek daimōn, a spirit or divine power, via Latin daemon, which later came to mean an evil spirit.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as DEE-mon with a long o in the second syllable, when the ending is a reduced schwa.
Confusing demon with daemon in computing, where daemon refers to a background process.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, demons are evil spirits opposed to God, and the Greek word is daimonion, a diminutive form related to daimon. The Gospels describe Jesus casting out demons, which shows his authority over evil. Mark 1:34 says Jesus healed many and cast out many demons. Matthew 12:24-28 records the Pharisees accusing Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebul, and Jesus answering that the kingdom of God has come upon them. James 2:19 says the demons believe and shudder, showing that belief alone is not enough.

demon.etymology: From Middle English *demon*, a borrowing from Medieval Latin *dēmōn*, *daemōn* (“lar, familiar spirit, guardian spirit”), from Ancient Greek *δαίμων* (“dispenser, god, protective spirit”).

senses.definition: The belief that the human being is formed of two components: material (body or flesh) and spiritual (soul or spirit).

core.definition: The view that a human being consists of two parts, body and soul (or spirit), rather than three.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAH. The 'ch' is a hard /k/, not 'ch' as in 'church'. The unstressed 'tuh' is a flapped t or schwa-like syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it names a position in a debate.
nuance.usage_note: Used in theology and philosophy of mind, in discussions of human nature. It is contrasted with trichotomism. In general talk, Americans would say 'the belief that people have a body and a soul'.

distinctions.note: Trichotomism holds that humans are body, soul and spirit, three distinct parts.
Monism holds that the person is a single unified substance, with no separate soul.
Dualism is broader, claiming mind and body are distinct, while dichotomism is the specific theological two-part view.

examples.everyday: My theology professor said most Christians through history have held to dichotomism, meaning body and soul.
examples.professional: The textbook chapter introduces dichotomism and trichotomism before moving to modern monist proposals.
examples.analytical: Dichotomism treats 'soul' and 'spirit' in Scripture as overlapping terms for the immaterial aspect of the person, set against the material body.

nuance.analogy: Like a coin with two sides, a person is body and soul together.
nuance.etymology: From Greek dichotomia, 'a cutting in two', from dicha, 'in two' + temnein, 'to cut'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'ch' like 'church' instead of /k/.
Confusing dichotomism with dichotomy, which is any division into two.
Treating it as the same as monism.
nuance.biblical_note: Dichotomists point to passages such as Matthew 10:28 (body and soul) and Genesis 2:7, and argue that 'soul' and 'spirit' are used interchangeably, as in Luke 1:46-47. Trichotomists point to 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and Hebrews 4:12, where spirit and soul are named separately.

senses.definition: To become less virulent or strong; to subside.
senses.example: We'll be able to sail safely across the bay once the storm dies down.

core.definition: To gradually become weaker, quieter, or less intense, such as a storm, a crowd, or a rumor.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DOWN, the particle, so say 'dy DOWN' with a clear down sound. In speech, 'die' keeps its diphthong and is not shortened.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a natural decline and is usually calm or reassuring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for weather, noise, arguments, rumors, or emotions. For example, people say 'Let's wait for the rain to die down' or 'Give the drama a few days to die down.' It is casual but fits most everyday and professional situations.

distinctions.note: Calm down is mainly for people's emotions, while die down is used for things like storms, noise, or rumors.
Subside is more formal and can be used for physical or emotional intensity, while die down is more casual.

collocations: wait for the rumors to die down

examples.everyday: Let's grab a coffee after the rain dies down.
examples.professional: Let's hold off on the launch until the complaints die down.
examples.analytical: Public outrage tends to die down once a scandal loses its novelty.

nuance.analogy: Like a campfire slowly fading to embers after the logs are burned.
common_mistakes: Using 'die' in the present when the subject is past, as in 'The rain die down' instead of 'The rain died down'.
Confusing 'die' with 'dye' in writing, since they sound the same.

conversation.text: We waited for the wind to die down before going out on the boat.
The rumors finally died down after a few weeks.

senses.definition: Not bright or colorful.
senses.example: The lighting was too dim for me to make out his facial features.

senses.definition: Not smart or intelligent.
senses.example: He may be a bit dim, but he's not entirely stupid.

senses.definition: Indistinct, hazy or unclear.
senses.example: His vision grew dimmer as he aged.

senses.definition: Disapproving, unfavorable: rarely used outside the phrase take a dim view of.
Clipping of diminished.
To make something less bright.
senses.example: He dimmed the lights and put on soft music.

senses.definition: To become darker.
senses.example: The lights dimmed briefly when the air conditioning was turned on.

senses.definition: To render dim, obscure, or dark; to make less bright or distinct.
To deprive of distinct vision; to hinder from seeing clearly, either by dazzling or clouding the eyes; to darken the senses or understanding of.
To diminish, dull, or curtail.
senses.example: All these setbacks had started to dim the hopes of the students.

core.definition: Not bright or easy to see; having little light, so that things are hard to make out.

pronunciation.tip: It is a single short syllable with a short 'i' as in 'bit.' Non-native speakers sometimes say 'deem,' which is a different word with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Mostly neutral or negative, describing poor light, weak vision, or a gloomy mood; it can be positive in 'dim sum' or soft lighting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'dim' for lights, rooms, and eyesight, as in 'The hallway light is dim.' It can also describe a person as not smart, but that use is informal and can sound rude. In restaurants, 'let's dim the lights' is a natural request.

distinctions.note: Faint describes something hard to see or hear because it is weak; dim describes low light or a dull appearance.
Dark means no or almost no light; dim means some light but not enough.

examples.everyday: The porch light is so dim that I can barely find the keys.
examples.professional: The monitor was too dim in the conference room, so we moved the presentation near the window.
examples.analytical: Paul writes that we now see in a mirror dimly, a metaphor for the limits of present human knowledge.

nuance.analogy: A dim light is like a candle in a big room: it helps a little, but you cannot see clearly.
nuance.etymology: From Old English dimm, meaning dark or obscure, related to Old Norse dimmr.
common_mistakes: Using 'dim' for 'deem' or saying 'dim' with a long vowel.
Saying 'more dimmer' instead of 'dimmer' (the comparative is already formed).
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses 'dim' for failing sight, such as Isaac's eyes in Genesis 27:1 (RSV), which were dim so that he could not see. In 1 Corinthians 13:12 (RSV) Paul says we now see in a mirror dimly, using the Greek word aἰnigma for 'riddle,' and contrasts this with seeing face to face later. The point is limited present knowledge compared with the fullness to come.

dim.etymology: From Middle English *dim*, *dym*, from Old English *dim*, *dimm* (“dim, dark, gloomy; wretched, grievous, sad, unhappy”), from **dimm*, from Proto-Germanic **dimmaz* (“dark”), from Proto-Indo-European **dʰem-* (“to whisk, smoke; obscure”).

senses.definition: The state of being out of proportion; an abnormal or improper ratio; an imbalance.
senses.example: the disproportion of the length of a building to its height

senses.definition: Lack of suitableness, adequacy, or due proportion to an end or use; unsuitableness.
senses.example: the disproportion of strength or means to an object

senses.definition: To make unsuitable in quantity, form, or fitness; to violate symmetry in; to mismatch.

core.definition: A lack of balance or proper size, relation, or ratio between things that should match.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'DIS'. The 'r' in each syllable is clearly pronounced, and the final syllable is a reduced 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it describes an imbalance that is usually a problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'disproportion' mainly in formal writing, analysis, or argument. In everyday speech, people more often say 'out of proportion' or 'unequal.' It is common in discussions of costs, benefits, or responsibilities.

distinctions.note: 'Imbalance' is common and general; 'disproportion' stresses a mismatch in size or ratio between related parts.
'Inequality' refers to unequal treatment or status; 'disproportion' is about mismatched sizes or amounts.

collocations: a disproportion between costs and benefits

examples.everyday: There's a real disproportion between what we pay for the rent and what the apartment is worth.
examples.professional: The report flagged a disproportion between our budget and the work the team is actually doing.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on a disproportion between the moral claim and the evidence offered for it.

nuance.analogy: A disproportion is like a giant shoe on a small foot: the parts no longer fit together.
nuance.etymology: From 'dis-' (not) plus 'proportion,' from Latin 'proportio.'
common_mistakes: Using 'disproportion' as a verb in everyday speech; it is usually a noun.
Saying 'in disproportion' instead of 'a disproportion' or 'out of proportion.'

senses.definition: Something that distracts.
senses.example: Poking one's eye is a good distraction from a hurting toe.

senses.definition: The process of being distracted.
senses.example: We have to reduce distraction in class if we want students to achieve good results.

senses.definition: Perturbation; disorder; disturbance; confusion.
Mental disarray; a deranged state of mind; insanity.
senses.example: The incessant nightmares drove him to distraction.

core.definition: Something that pulls your attention away from what you are doing or thinking about.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the -TRAK- syllable, and the -tion ending is pronounced shun, not shin. The vowel in the first syllable is a reduced schwa-like sound.

nuance.connotation: Usually neutral to mildly negative, because a distraction interrupts something you need to do. It can be positive when it is a welcome break.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'That's a distraction' or 'Let's avoid distractions' in meetings and at work. A pleasant break is often called a welcome distraction, which is a natural and friendly phrase. The idiom 'driven to distraction' means to be so annoyed or stressed that you cannot think clearly.

distinctions.note: An interruption breaks into a conversation or process, while a distraction is anything that pulls your attention, even silently.
A diversion can be a planned or enjoyable change of activity, while a distraction is usually unplanned and interferes with focus.
A disturbance is a broader disruption to order or peace, often more serious than a distraction.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the pool was a nice distraction from the heat and all the errands.
examples.professional: Let's turn off notifications during the review so there are fewer distractions.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard warns that the crowd can become a distraction that hides the question of the self.

nuance.analogy: A distraction is like a pop-up ad on a web page you are trying to read: it grabs your eyes even when you did not ask for it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin distractio, a pulling apart, from distrahere.
common_mistakes: Using distraction as a verb; the verb is distract.
Using distraction to mean emotional distress; the closer word is distress.
Stressing the wrong syllable as dis-TRAK-shun or dis-trak-SHUN.

distraction.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *distraction*, from Latin *distractio*.

senses.definition: To make (something) diverse or varied in form or quality; to give variety to (something) to distinguish by numerous aspects or differences.
To make the scope of (business, investments, etc.) diverse, especially so as to balance and mitigate risks.

core.definition: To make something more varied, or to spread a business or investments across several areas to reduce risk.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the final syllable rhymes with my. The -si- in the middle is a quick suh sound, not a long see.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes a planned change toward variety or safety.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use diversify in business and investing, and in general speech about variety. For example, a company may diversify its products, or a person may diversify their investments. It is common in news and corporate writing.

distinctions.note: Vary means to change or be different over time; diversify implies a deliberate effort to add variety.
Expand means to grow in size; diversify means to add different kinds of things, not just more of the same.

examples.everyday: I'm trying to diversify my cooking so I don't make the same three dinners every week.
examples.professional: We need to diversify our client base so one contract loss won't hurt the whole division.
examples.analytical: The author argues that a healthy intellectual culture must diversify its sources rather than rely on a single authority.
