senses.definition: A small flying insect of the family Culicidae, the females of which bite humans and animals and suck blood, leaving an itching bump on the skin, and sometimes carrying diseases like malaria, dengue and yellow fever.
To fly close to the ground, seemingly without a course.

core.definition: A small flying insect whose female bites people and animals to drink blood, leaving an itchy bump and sometimes spreading diseases like malaria.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SKEE, and the final syllable is a light 'toh' with no extra vowel. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or add an extra 'o' sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: negative, because the insect is associated with itchy bites and disease; the word itself is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word constantly in summer talk about bug bites, camping, and mosquito spray. The plural is mosquitoes, not mosquitos. The verb sense meaning to fly aimlessly is rare in everyday American speech.

distinctions.note: A gnat is a much smaller fly that does not bite people, while a mosquito is a biting insect that drinks blood.
Fly is the general word for many winged insects, while mosquito names one specific biting group.

examples.everyday: Bring some bug spray, because the mosquitoes are brutal by the lake this time of year.
examples.professional: Facilities says the county mosquito control crew will treat the drainage ditches behind our parking lot next Thursday.
examples.analytical: The mosquito shows how an insect smaller than a fingernail has shaped human history more than many large predators have.

nuance.analogy: A mosquito is like a tiny uninvited guest who takes a little something from you and leaves a mark behind.
nuance.etymology: From Spanish and Portuguese, meaning little fly, from mosca (fly).
common_mistakes: Saying mosquitos instead of mosquitoes in the plural.
Stressing the first syllable as MOS-quito instead of muh-SKEE-toh.

mosquito.etymology: Spanish *mosquito* (“gnat”), diminutive of *mosca* (“fly”), from Latin *musca* (“fly”), from Proto-Indo-European **mūs-* (“fly, stinging fly, gnat”).

conversation.text: I got like twenty mosquito bites last night.
The mosquitoes are terrible by the lake at sunset.
Close the screen door, or the mosquitoes will get in.

senses.definition: A neural network having at least one hidden layer, and whose neurons use a nonlinear activation function (e.g. sigmoid).

core.definition: A feedforward neural network with one or more hidden layers of nonlinear neurons, used for classification and regression.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LAY and on PUR, so the middle syllables stay light. Keep the r in 'layer' and 'perceptron' (American rhotic r), and don't turn the final syllable into 'tron' with a long o.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and AI engineers use this term in technical discussions, papers and model design reviews. Colleagues often shorten it to MLP or say 'a simple neural net' in casual talk. In a meeting, you can say 'Let's start with a multilayer perceptron as the baseline.'

distinctions.note: A single-layer perceptron has no hidden layer and can only separate linearly separable patterns; a multilayer perceptron can learn nonlinear boundaries.
Deep network is the broader term for networks with many layers, including convolutional and transformer models; MLP usually means a fully connected feedforward model.

collocations: hidden layer of a multilayer perceptron

examples.everyday: My friend who works at a bank said her team built a multilayer perceptron to flag suspicious transactions.
examples.professional: Let's try a multilayer perceptron with two hidden layers as a baseline before we move to the transformer model.
examples.analytical: A multilayer perceptron with nonlinear activations can approximate any continuous function on a compact set, given enough hidden units.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay of filters, where each layer transforms the signal before passing it to the next.
nuance.etymology: Multilayer from multi- (Latin multus, many) plus layer; perceptron was coined by Frank Rosenblatt from perception plus -tron.
common_mistakes: Saying 'multiple layer perceptron' instead of the standard term 'multilayer perceptron'.
Confusing a single perceptron unit with a multilayer network.

conversation.text: A multilayer perceptron has one or more hidden layers of fully connected units with nonlinear activations.
Inside each transformer block, there's a small multilayer perceptron applied to every token.
Let's try a two-layer multilayer perceptron on the embeddings before fine-tuning the whole model.

senses.definition: Of, characterized by, or pertaining to murder or murderers.
Of a person: intending or likely to commit murder; bloodthirsty, homicidal.
senses.example: murderous behavior

senses.definition: Of an object: used to commit murder; capable of causing death; deadly, fatal.
Very difficult.
senses.example: a murderous exam

core.definition: Intending or capable of killing; bloodthirsty, deadly, or fatal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the last two syllables as weak, quick sounds. It is three syllables, not 'mur-DER-us.' The middle vowel is a reduced 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: strongly negative. It describes intent or capacity to kill, or an extreme, violent anger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'murderous' for a person with murderous intent, or for something deadly, such as a murderous storm or road. It can also be used figuratively for extreme anger, as in 'a murderous glare,' though it is strong. In everyday speech, a person might say 'she gave me a murderous look' jokingly, but it should be used carefully.

distinctions.note: Deadly is common and can describe a thing that can kill or a serious situation; murderous emphasizes intent or violence.
Homicidal is clinical or legal and describes the tendency to kill; murderous is more vivid and everyday.

examples.everyday: He gave me a murderous look when I took the last slice of pizza.
examples.professional: The engineering team flagged a bug that could cause murderous delays if the system were deployed.
examples.analytical: The author argues that murderous ideologies grow when people are persuaded that others are not fully human.

nuance.analogy: A murderous rage is like a fire that spreads without control, destroying whatever is in its path.
nuance.etymology: From murder plus the adjective suffix -ous, from Old English morðor.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'murderous' with 'murderer'; the adjective describes intent or capacity, not the person.
Stressing the wrong syllable, or pronouncing it with an extra syllable.

senses.definition: The doctrines, principles, or practice of a mystagogue; interpretation of mysteries.

core.definition: The teaching and initiation of new members into the inner meaning of religious mysteries, especially the sacraments and the rites of worship.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MIS, and the final -gy is pronounced like 'jee'. Learners often stress the second syllable or pronounce the g as a hard sound in the last part.

nuance.connotation: neutral, a technical term from church history and theology with a reverent tone
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mystagogy almost only in academic theology, church history, or Orthodox and liturgical studies. It is not used in everyday talk. A person who does this teaching is called a mystagogue, and the word is most common in discussions of early Christian catechesis.

distinctions.note: Catechesis is basic instruction in Christian belief for new believers, while mystagogy focuses on the deeper, sacramental meaning revealed after initiation.
Mysticism is direct experience of God, while mystagogy is the teaching or guiding that leads people into those sacred mysteries.

examples.everyday: My pastor said the deeper mystagogy of communion takes years to understand, not just one class.
examples.professional: In our seminary course, we will read the fourth-century mystagogy lectures alongside the liturgy.
examples.analytical: Cyril's mystagogy presents baptism not merely as an initial rite but as an entry into the hidden meaning of the sacrament.

nuance.analogy: If catechesis is learning the alphabet of faith, mystagogy is reading the deeper poetry hidden inside the words.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mystagōgia, from mystagōgos, a guide who leads initiates into the mysteries.
common_mistakes: Confusing mystagogy with mystery or mysticism, which are related but not the same meaning.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying mis-TAG-uh-jee instead of MIS-tuh-goh-jee.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of narrow artificial intelligence.

core.definition: AI designed to perform one specific task or a small set of tasks, such as spam filtering or face recognition; all AI in use today.

pronunciation.tip: Stress NAR in narrow, then give AI its own main stress when you say the letters A and I. Say the letters clearly and do not read AI as the word eye.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a technical classification and does not imply praise or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use narrow AI in tech, business and news discussions to separate today's task-specific systems from hypothetical general AI. Spell out the letters A and I when speaking. In casual talk people often just say AI, and narrow AI appears mainly when the difference matters.

distinctions.note: General AI would match human flexibility across many tasks, while narrow AI excels only within a defined domain.
Machine learning is a method for building systems from data, while narrow AI describes what the system is designed to do.

examples.everyday: Most of the AI on my phone is narrow AI, like the face unlock or the photo sorting.
examples.professional: Our roadmap focuses on narrow AI tools that match invoices to purchase orders, not on general AI.
examples.analytical: Narrow AI systems can outperform experts within bounded domains, yet they lack the transfer of understanding that marks general intelligence.

nuance.analogy: Narrow AI is like a calculator: astonishingly fast at arithmetic, but unable to write a poem or make a joke.
nuance.etymology: Narrow from Old English nearu 'tight, confined'; AI from artificial intelligence, a term coined in 1955.
common_mistakes: Saying the letters A and I as one word, like a-eye, instead of two distinct letters.
Confusing narrow AI with narrow-minded or implying the technology is limited in quality rather than scope.

conversation.text: A spam filter is a good example of narrow AI: excellent at one task, useless at others.
Everything we've deployed so far is narrow AI, trained for a specific business problem.
Narrow AI can beat experts at chess and still fail at tasks a child finds trivial.

senses.definition: The cry of a horse.
To make its cry.
To make a sound similar to a horse's cry.

core.definition: The loud, high-pitched cry a horse makes.

pronunciation.tip: Use one syllable with a long 'ay' sound. The stress is on this only syllable, and the final sound is a clear 'ay' not an 'ee.'

nuance.connotation: neutral, a sound description.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use neigh for a horse's sound in everyday speech, in children's books, and in description. It is a simple, widely understood word. Used as a verb, it is also common in writing about animals.

distinctions.note: Whinny is a softer, quieter sound, often a friendly call, while neigh is the louder, more powerful cry.
Snort is a sharp burst of air through the nose, not a vocal cry.

collocations: the horse let out a neigh

examples.everyday: When we pulled up to the barn, the horse gave a loud neigh and trotted to the fence.
examples.professional: In the field report, the observer noted that a neigh from the stable signaled the animal's distress.
examples.analytical: The poet's line gives the neigh of the stallion a fierce, almost human urgency.

nuance.analogy: A neigh is like a car horn for a horse: a loud, sharp call that announces its presence.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hnǣgan, an imitation of the sound.
common_mistakes: Confusing neigh with 'nay,' which means 'no' or is a different word.
Pronouncing it with an 'ee' sound instead of a clear 'ay.'

neigh.etymology: Middle English *neyen*, from Old English *hnǣġan*, from **hnaijan*, from Proto-Germanic **hnajjaną* (“to neigh”).

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see not,‎ much.
senses.example: There's not much meat in this chicken curry.

senses.definition: Used sarcastically with opposite meaning to express strong agreement or assertion of truth; a lot.
senses.example: "She's rich, is she?" — "Huh, not much!" [meaning yes, she is very rich]

core.definition: Very little or nothing special; used to say that little is happening or that there is only a small amount of something.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on MUCH, and 'not' is quick and light. In casual speech 'not much' often sounds like 'nah-MUCH,' so do not pronounce the 't' in 'not' too crisply.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it is a casual, low-key reply that can sound uninterested if said flatly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'not much' as a casual reply to 'What's up?' or 'What have you been doing?' Saying 'Not much, just relaxing' is friendly and normal. It can also mean there is little of something, as in 'There's not much left.'

distinctions.note: 'Not many' is used with countable nouns, while 'not much' is used with uncountable nouns or amounts.
'Not a lot' is more casual and common in speech, while 'not much' is slightly more neutral and can be used in more formal contexts.

examples.everyday: What did you do this weekend? Not much, just watched some movies and cleaned the apartment.
examples.professional: There's not much movement on the ticket since Monday, so I'll follow up with the vendor tomorrow.
examples.analytical: The author's claim that the evidence is 'not much' depends on how one weighs small effect sizes against the large sample.

nuance.analogy: Like a half-empty glass that is still a little full, 'not much' means there is less than expected but not absolutely none.
common_mistakes: Using 'not much' with countable nouns; say 'not many friends' rather than 'not much friends.'
Saying 'not much' as a flat reply without warmth, which can sound rude.

conversation.text: "What's up?" "Not much. Just hanging out at home."
"What did you do this weekend?" "Not much, honestly. I mostly slept."
There's not much going on at work this week, which is kind of nice.

senses.definition: Not parallel or perpendicular to the base.
senses.example: Italic fonts are sometimes described as oblique in typographic terminology.

senses.definition: Not straightforward; indirect; by implication; obscure, ambiguous, or confusing.
senses.example: The email from HR obliquely informed her that some complaints about her had been received.

senses.definition: Disingenuous, underhand, morally corrupt.
Not direct in descent; not following the line of father and son; collateral.
Relating to the oblique case.

Indirect; employing the actual words of the speaker but as related by a third person, having the first person in pronoun and verb converted into the third person and adverbs of present time into the past, etc.
senses.example: They found out obliquely that she had heard from HR about the comments and was taking some time to absorb the sting of an implied reprimand.

senses.definition: Of a leaf, having the base of the blade asymmetrical, with one side lower than the other.
Growing at an angle that is neither vertical nor horizontal.
Employing oblique motion, motion or progression in which one part (voice) stays on the same note while another ascends or descends.
An oblique line.
Synonym of slash: the typographic mark ⟨/⟩.
Ellipsis of oblique case.
The musculus obliquus externus abdominis or obliquus internus abdominis.
To deviate from a perpendicular line; to become askew.
To slant (text, etc.) at an angle.
To march in a direction oblique to the line of the column or platoon; — formerly accomplished by oblique steps, now by direct steps, the men half-facing either to the right or left.

core.definition: Slanted or indirect; not straight up-and-down or side-to-side, or not stated openly and directly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, BLEEK, and the final vowel is a long ee sound, not a short i. The first syllable is an unstressed oh, so do not add an extra syllable at the start.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical senses such as angles and lines; in the figurative sense of an indirect remark, it is neutral to mildly negative, suggesting evasiveness.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, oblique is used mostly for figurative meanings, like an oblique comment or an oblique reference, which means something hinted at rather than said plainly. Americans use it in writing, academic talk and formal discussion more than in casual chat. For physical slant, people usually say diagonal or slanted instead.

distinctions.note: Indirect is the everyday word for not going straight to a point; oblique is more literary and suggests a deliberate avoidance of plain statement.
Diagonal describes a line across a square or grid; oblique is broader and can describe any non-right angle, including in figurative use.
Ambiguous means having more than one possible meaning; oblique means approached indirectly, which may or may not be unclear.

examples.everyday: When I asked if she was coming to the party, she gave an oblique answer about being busy that week.
examples.professional: The client's email made an oblique reference to budget cuts, so I asked the project manager to clarify directly.
examples.analytical: The author's oblique treatment of divine silence invites the reader to infer a theology of mystery rather than state one outright.

nuance.analogy: An oblique remark is like a path that bends around a point instead of walking straight at it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obliquus, meaning slanting or sideways.
common_mistakes: Using oblique to mean only a diagonal physical line in everyday speech, where diagonal is more natural.
Stressing the first syllable (OH-blique) instead of the second.

senses.definition: Of property or real estate: adjacent to the ocean.
A property that is adjacent to the ocean.
The side of a property that faces the ocean.

core.definition: Located directly on the ocean shore, with a view of or direct access to the ocean.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, OH, and let the second syllable be a weak schwa. The compound's second stress is lighter on front, so do not pronounce each part fully.

nuance.connotation: positive in real estate, suggesting a desirable location with views.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use oceanfront most often in real estate ads, vacation rentals, and everyday talk about beach towns. A condo listing might say oceanfront unit, while a local would just say on the beach. It is also used as a noun, as in buying oceanfront, and is natural in both casual and business settings.

distinctions.note: Beachfront usually means located next to the beach, which might be on a lake or river; oceanfront specifically means the ocean.
Oceanside is a more relaxed term and often means on the ocean side of a town or area; oceanfront usually means directly on the water.

examples.everyday: We booked an oceanfront room so we could wake up and see the waves every morning.
examples.professional: The property team expects strong demand for the oceanfront units this season.
examples.analytical: Coastal planners debate whether oceanfront development should be restricted as sea levels rise.

nuance.analogy: Like a front porch that faces the street, oceanfront describes the side of the property that faces the water.
nuance.etymology: Compound of ocean and front.
common_mistakes: Writing oceanfront as two words in American writing; the standard form is one word.
Using oceanfront for a location near the sea but not directly on it; oceanview is more accurate in that case.

conversation.text: We splurged on an oceanfront room, and the view was totally worth it.
Is the condo oceanfront, or do we have to walk to the beach?
Oceanfront hotels are way more expensive during the summer.

senses.definition: Using the phone's speaker so others in the room can hear.

core.definition: Using the phone's speaker so that other people in the room can hear the call.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPEAK, the first syllable of speaker. Say the final -er as a clear American r-colored vowel (kur), not 'speaker' with a separate ah-sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday phrase with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this constantly at work and at home, often at the start of a call: 'Hang on, I'm putting you on speaker.' Always say it before you put a call on speaker, so people nearby are not surprised by a voice. A natural reply is 'Got it' or 'Hi everyone.'

distinctions.note: On speaker means others can hear; on mute means your microphone is off so others cannot hear you.
Speakerphone is the device or feature itself; on speaker describes the state of a call using it.

examples.everyday: Hang on, I'm putting you on speaker so Mom can hear too.
examples.professional: Dana, I'm dialing in from the car, so I'll put you on speaker for the standup.
examples.analytical: A call placed on speaker changes who is party to the conversation, which raises questions about confidentiality.

nuance.analogy: Like turning up a radio so the whole kitchen can hear the song instead of holding it to one ear.
nuance.etymology: Combines the preposition on with speaker, from speak (Old English specan).
common_mistakes: Saying 'in speaker' instead of 'on speaker'.
Forgetting to warn people before switching a call to speaker.

conversation.text: Just so you know, you're on speaker; the whole team is here.
I'm driving, so I have you on speaker.
Sorry, the kids can hear everything; you're on speaker.

senses.definition: Of food or food products, grown in an environment free from artificial agrichemicals, and possibly certified by a regulatory body.

Describing a form of social solidarity theorized by Emile Durkheim that is characterized by voluntary engagements in complex interdependencies for mutual benefit (such as business agreements), rather than mechanical solidarity, which depends on ascribed relations between people (as in a family or tribe).
Instrumental; acting as instruments of nature or of art to a certain destined function or end.
Generated according to the ranking algorithms of a search engine, as opposed to deliberate promotional techniques e.g. by advertisers.
Developing in a gradual or natural fashion.
senses.example: The writing of the script was an organic process.

senses.definition: Harmonious; coherent; structured.
senses.example: The production came together in an organic whole.

senses.definition: Pertaining to or derived from living organisms.
Pertaining to an organ of the body of a living organism.
Relating to the compounds of carbon, relating to natural products.
Of a military unit or formation, or its elements, belonging to a permanent organization (in contrast to being temporarily attached).
An organic food.
A living organism, as opposed to a robot or hologram.
An organic compound.

core.definition: Describing food grown without synthetic pesticides, herbicides, or fertilizers, and certified under a government standard such as USDA Organic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GAN, the second syllable. The first syllable is a short, reduced vowel, so do not say OR-ganic or or-GAY-nik.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most American contexts, suggesting healthy, natural, and environmentally friendly food, though some people see it as expensive or marketed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use organic very often in grocery stores, restaurants, and conversations about health. A USDA Organic label means the product meets federal standards, so the word has a legal meaning in the United States. People often say organic eggs or organic produce, and a common reply to an offer is Yes, is it organic?

distinctions.note: Natural is a loose marketing term without a strict legal definition, while organic has a regulated meaning under USDA rules.
Free-range describes how animals are raised, while organic describes how the food is grown and certified.

examples.everyday: Are these tomatoes organic, or should I get the regular ones?
examples.professional: Our client wants the new product line certified organic, so we need the supplier to provide the USDA documentation.
examples.analytical: The label organic carries a regulatory meaning, but its health benefits are contested in the research literature, which complicates its marketing claims.

nuance.analogy: Organic food is like a garden grown by hand without chemical sprays, while conventional food is like a field managed with industrial tools.
nuance.etymology: From Latin organicus, relating to an organ or instrument, later used for living things.
common_mistakes: Saying organic meaning natural in every sense, when the American label has a legal definition.
Pronouncing the first syllable as OR, which sounds too strong; the stress is on GAN.

organic.etymology: From Middle English *organic*, *organik*, from Old French *organique*, from Latin *organicus*.

conversation.text: We try to buy organic fruit when we can.
Organic eggs cost more at the store.
Is this salad made with organic vegetables?

senses.definition: A person who studies or practices ornithology.

core.definition: A scientist or expert who studies birds, including their behavior, anatomy, classification, and habitats.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, THAH. The th is voiceless, as in 'thin', and the last syllable is reduced to an unstressed ih sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes an expert in a scientific field.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ornithologist for professional scientists and academics. A hobbyist who watches birds is usually called a birder, and that word is more natural in casual talk. For a university or museum role, ornithologist is the standard title.

distinctions.note: A birder is an enthusiast who watches birds for pleasure, while an ornithologist is a trained scientist who studies birds.
A zoologist studies animals in general, while an ornithologist specializes in birds.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a bird watcher, but she calls herself a birder, not an ornithologist.
examples.professional: The park hired an ornithologist to count the migrating species each spring.
examples.analytical: An ornithologist must distinguish between observed behavior and inherited patterns when explaining migration.

nuance.analogy: An ornithologist is to birds what a geologist is to rocks: a trained expert who studies one kind of living thing closely.
nuance.etymology: From Greek ornis, bird, and -logist, one who studies.
common_mistakes: Using ornithologist for any bird lover; in casual American speech, birder is more natural.
Mispronouncing the th as a t or d sound.

senses.definition: To cast out; to banish.
That has been cast out; banished, ostracized.
One that has been excluded from a society or a system, a pariah, a leper.
senses.example: If ever you chance upon the whole truth about any outcast or many, never tell it to just anybody, or at least not right away; unjust exclusion from a society is just one kind of hardship.

senses.definition: Synonym of outsider: someone who does not belong, a misfit.
The amount of increase in the bulk of grain during malting.

core.definition: A person who is rejected or excluded from a group, family, or society and treated as an outsider.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, OUT. The vowel in "cast" is the short a of "cat," not the "ah" of "father."

nuance.connotation: Negative or sad. It describes someone who is pushed away, sometimes unfairly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "outcast" for people who are socially rejected, such as a student excluded by classmates or a family member cut off. It is common in books, films, and serious conversation. As an adjective, it is mainly literary and rare in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: An outsider simply does not belong to a group. An outcast has been actively rejected and pushed out.
A misfit is someone who does not fit in because of personality or style, often lightly. An outcast implies a more serious exclusion.

examples.everyday: After the argument, she felt like an outcast in her own friend group.
examples.professional: A team member who is treated as an outcast will rarely share ideas in meetings.
examples.analytical: The prophet's reflections on the outcast reveal how communities define belonging by excluding those who challenge their norms.

nuance.analogy: Like a plant pulled out of a garden bed, an outcast has been removed from the place where they belong.
nuance.etymology: From out and cast.
common_mistakes: Using "outcast" as a verb in everyday speech; the usual verb phrase is "cast out."
Stressing the second syllable, which sounds wrong for the noun.
Confusing it with "outsider," which is much milder.

senses.definition: An ornament worn hanging on the breast by Russian bishops.

core.definition: A small icon of the Virgin Mary worn on the chest by Eastern Orthodox bishops as a sign of their office.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, -JEE-. The j is pronounced like the 'j' in 'jam', and the final -a is a soft 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a specialized religious term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use panagia mainly in Orthodox church settings, theological writing or conversations about church vestments. Most people outside Orthodoxy will not know the word, so explain it as a bishop's icon of Mary. Eastern Orthodox speakers may use the Greek or Slavic term, and English-speaking Orthodox usually say panagia.

distinctions.note: A pectoral cross is a cross worn on the chest; a panagia is an icon of the Virgin Mary worn in a similar position.
An icon is any sacred image; a panagia is a specific icon worn by bishops.

examples.everyday: At the liturgy, the bishop wore a gold panagia that caught the light.
examples.professional: In the vestment catalog, the panagia is listed as a standard item for Orthodox hierarchs.
examples.analytical: The panagia signifies the bishop's dedication to the Mother of God and his pastoral care of the flock.

nuance.analogy: Like a badge of office worn over the heart, carrying an image of the Mother of God.
nuance.etymology: From Greek panagia, all-holy, from pan, all, and hagios, holy, a title of the Virgin Mary.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as PAN-uh-jee-uh.
Thinking it is a general word for any Marian image; it refers to the bishop's chest icon.

senses.definition: Capable of being pardoned; worthy of pardon.

core.definition: Able to be forgiven; deserving of forgiveness, especially for a mistake or a minor offense.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PAR, and the ending -able is reduced to a weak 'uh-bul' sound. Learners often add an extra 'ay' sound (pardon-AY-ble), which is not used in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It signals understanding and fairness toward someone who has done wrong, and it is often used to soften criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pardonable' mostly in phrases like 'a pardonable mistake' or 'a pardonable error' to say that a mistake is understandable and should be forgiven. You will hear it in workplace feedback, in apologies, and in everyday conversation about small errors. For serious wrongdoing, Americans usually say 'forgivable' or 'excusable' instead, and they rarely describe a crime as pardonable.

distinctions.note: 'Forgivable' focuses on whether the person can be forgiven emotionally, while 'pardonable' suggests that the act is excusable enough to be let go without punishment.
'Excusable' stresses that there are reasons that explain the behavior, whereas 'pardonable' emphasizes that the person deserves to be forgiven.

examples.everyday: You spilled coffee on the table, but that's pardonable, so don't worry about it.
examples.professional: Missing one deadline during the server migration was pardonable, but missing three would need a conversation with the manager.
examples.analytical: Some theologians argue that a sin may be pardonable in the eyes of God even when it remains morally serious and must be repented.

nuance.analogy: A pardonable mistake is like a small stain on a shirt that a friend laughs off, because it is understandable and does not ruin the relationship.
nuance.etymology: From Old French pardoner, from Latin perdonare, 'to give up entirely, forgive'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long 'ay' in the last syllable, as in 'pardon-AY-ble'.
Using it for serious crimes, where 'forgivable' or 'excusable' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: A small stone, especially one rounded by the action of water.
A small droplet of water intentionally sprayed on the ice that cause irregularities on the surface.
Transparent and colorless rock crystal.
senses.example: Brazilian pebble

senses.definition: A form of slow-burning gunpowder in large cubical grains.
A small piece of crack cocaine.
A particle from 4 to 64 mm in diameter, following the Wentworth scale.
To pave with pebbles.
To deposit water droplets on the ice.
senses.example: to pebble the ice between games

senses.definition: To give (leather) a rough appearance with small rounded prominences.
To place a pebble at (a vertex of a graph) according to certain rules, in a pebble game.

core.definition: A small, smooth stone, usually rounded by the action of water or sand.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced 'uhl' with a syllabic l. Avoid adding a separate vowel between b and l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a small natural object, sometimes with a playful or peaceful image.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pebble in everyday talk about beaches, gardens, shoes, and walking paths. It is a plain word, and it is commonly used in phrases about small things adding up. For a larger stone, Americans say rock or boulder.

distinctions.note: Rock is larger and more general; pebble is small and usually smooth.
Gravel is a collection of small stones used for roads or paths; pebble refers to one stone.
Stone is general and can mean any piece of rock; pebble is specifically small and smooth.

examples.everyday: Our kids love collecting pebbles on the beach and skipping them across the water.
examples.professional: The site engineers flagged loose pebbles on the pathway, so we need to add a retaining edge.
examples.analytical: The sediment consists mainly of pebbles, whose rounding indicates long transport by water.

nuance.analogy: A pebble is like a small worn tooth of the earth, shaped by years of water.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'papol' or a related form, probably imitative of the sound of stones rattling.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel as a long 'ee' sound.
Using pebble for a large stone or boulder.
nuance.biblical_note: In 1 Samuel 17:40, David chooses five smooth stones from a brook for his sling before facing Goliath. The RSV uses 'stones' rather than 'pebbles', but the image of small, smooth stones is the same.

pebble.etymology: From Middle English *pibel* (also in *pibleston*), from Old English *papol-stān* (“pebble-stone”), from Old English **papol*, **pyppel*, **pæbbel* of origin + Old English *stān*.

senses.definition: The state or period of being a person.
The status of being considered as a person.
senses.example: A majority of the present world's peoples delay the conferral of personhood (to children).

core.definition: The state of being a person, or the status of being recognized as a person with rights and moral worth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle 'son' is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'sun', and the final 'hood' rhymes with 'good'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to serious. It is often used in debates about ethics, rights, and the start or end of life, so it can carry strong feelings in those settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'personhood' in discussions of ethics, law, medicine, and religion, often in debates about abortion, embryos, or artificial intelligence. It is not usually used in casual talk about someone's character. For a person's character, Americans say 'personality' or 'character'.

distinctions.note: Personality means a person's traits and temperament, while personhood means the status or state of being a person.
Humanity refers to the human race or to human kindness, while personhood focuses on the status of being a person with moral standing.

examples.everyday: My neighbor and I had a long talk about whether personhood starts at conception, and we disagreed politely.
examples.professional: The policy team needs a clear definition of personhood before we decide which records the new privacy rules cover.
examples.analytical: If personhood is grounded in rational capacity, then the question of who counts as a person becomes a question about the criteria we accept.

nuance.analogy: Personhood is like a passport: it does not describe who you are, but it grants you a status that others must recognize.
nuance.etymology: From person, from Latin persona, plus the Old English suffix -hood, meaning state or condition.
common_mistakes: Using 'personhood' to mean personality or character.
Stressing the wrong syllable or pronouncing the final 'hood' as 'hud'.

senses.definition: A practitioner of physic, i.e. a specialist in internal medicine, especially as opposed to a surgeon; a practitioner who treats with medication rather than with surgery.
A medical doctor trained in human medicine.

core.definition: A medical doctor who diagnoses and treats illness, usually through medication and non-surgical care.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, ZISH. The first vowel is a short i, not a long e, and the final syllable is a reduced schwa, so the word ends in -shun.

nuance.connotation: neutral to positive. It sounds respectful and professional, especially in written or formal contexts.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people usually say doctor, and a physician is what you call the doctor in formal writing, insurance paperwork, or medical contexts. You will hear primary care physician, family physician, or board-certified physician. Using physician to a friend in casual talk can sound stiff, but it is perfectly correct.

distinctions.note: Doctor is the everyday word and can also mean holders of a PhD. Physician specifically means a medical doctor.
A surgeon is a physician who performs operations, while a physician in the narrow sense treats mainly with medication and non-surgical care.

examples.everyday: You should call your physician if the fever lasts more than three days.
examples.professional: Our health plan requires that a physician sign off on the referral before the claim is processed.
examples.analytical: The Hippocratic tradition defined the physician less by cure than by a duty to do no harm to the sick.

nuance.analogy: A physician is the doctor who acts like a skilled pharmacist and diagnostician, while a surgeon is the one who picks up the scalpel.
nuance.etymology: From Latin physicus, from Greek physikos, meaning relating to nature; the medical sense developed in Middle English.
common_mistakes: Using physician for a PhD scientist, which Americans would find confusing; use doctor or scientist instead.
Pronouncing the first vowel as a long e (fee-ZISH-un) instead of a short i.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word iatros means physician. Colossians 4:14 calls Luke the beloved physician, and Mark 5:26 describes a woman who had suffered much under many physicians without being healed. Jeremiah 8:22 asks whether there is no physician in Gilead, using the image of healing for spiritual and national sickness.

physician.etymology: From Middle English *fisicien*, from Old French *fisicïen* (“physician”), from *fisique* (“art of healing”), from Latin *physica* (“natural science”), from Ancient Greek *φυσική ἐπιστήμη* (“knowledge of nature”), from *φυσικός* (“pertaining to nature”).

conversation.text: The clinic has three physicians and a nurse practitioner.
With an HMO, your primary care physician usually has to give you a referral.
She's been our family physician for almost twenty years.

senses.definition: To accept a bill and pay it, especially at a bar or restaurant.

core.definition: To accept the bill and pay for everyone's food or drinks, especially in a restaurant or bar.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on tab. Pick up links into pi-KUP, and the in the phrase reduces to thuh before a consonant.

nuance.connotation: positive. It describes generosity and treating others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say pick up the tab after dinner or drinks with friends, colleagues, or family. Pick up the check is also common in restaurants. A natural reply is Thanks, I owe you one, or Let me get the next one. If the group splits the bill, Americans say split the bill or go Dutch, so do not assume the phrase means everyone pays.

distinctions.note: Treat means to pay for someone as a gift, while pick up the tab is a more general phrase for paying the bill for a group.
Split the bill means everyone pays a share, while pick up the tab means one person pays the whole bill.

collocations: pick up the tab for dinner
offered to pick up the tab
I'll pick up the tab this time

examples.everyday: Dinner's on me tonight, so I'll pick up the tab, and you can get the next round.
examples.professional: Our vendor offered to pick up the tab for the team lunch after the client review.
examples.analytical: In social exchanges, whoever picks up the tab often gains a claim on gratitude, which can shape the relationship beyond the meal.

nuance.analogy: Picking up the tab is like grabbing the check at a family table and quietly making it clear that you'll handle the bill.
common_mistakes: Saying pay the tab in the sense of picking up the bill, which is less natural in American speech.
Using pick up the tab when you mean to split the bill; the phrase means one person pays the whole thing.

conversation.text: My boss picked up the tab for the whole team.
Let me pick up the tab this time.
Who's picking up the tab tonight?

senses.definition: Of a distribution: having kurtosis less than that of a normal distribution; equivalently, having negative excess kurtosis.

core.definition: Describing a statistical distribution whose peak is flatter and whose tails are thinner than a normal distribution, meaning negative excess kurtosis.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the third syllable, KUR, and the final -tic is short and unstressed. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or pronounce the middle vowel as a clear long ee, so keep it a quick, reduced ih.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a precise descriptive term with no positive or negative value; it only describes shape.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in statistics, data science, finance and research writing, usually when describing a histogram or distribution. In a meeting you might say the data looks platykurtic after someone asks about the tails. Outside technical talk, people say flat or spread out. Its opposite is leptokurtic.

distinctions.note: Leptokurtic describes a sharper peak and heavier tails, the opposite of platykurtic.
Mesokurtic describes a distribution with kurtosis equal to a normal distribution, so it is neither flat nor peaked.

examples.everyday: My kid's test scores look platykurtic, so most students landed near the average.
examples.professional: The residuals look platykurtic, so the normality assumption is probably fine for this model.
examples.analytical: A platykurtic distribution has lighter tails than the normal curve, which changes how we interpret extreme outcomes.

nuance.analogy: Think of a normal bell curve as a hill. A platykurtic distribution is a flatter, wider hill with fewer surprises out in the tails.
nuance.etymology: From Greek platys (broad, flat) and kyrtos (curved, bulging).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (PLAT-ee-kur-tik) instead of the middle KUR.
Confusing platykurtic with leptokurtic, which means the opposite.

senses.definition: The study of the Holy Spirit as revealed in Scripture.
The study of spiritual beings and phenomena, especially the interactions between humans and God.
The science dealing with air or gases, their physical and chemical properties, therapeutic applications, etc.

core.definition: The branch of theology that studies the Holy Spirit, especially as revealed in Scripture and in the life of the church.

pronunciation.tip: The initial 'p' is silent. Stress falls on the third syllable, -TAH-, with the American 'ah' vowel. The 'gy' ending is pronounced 'jee', and the 'ol' syllable is reduced to 'uh-luh'.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pneumatology mainly in seminaries, theology courses, and academic writing. In a church setting, people usually speak of 'the doctrine of the Holy Spirit' or 'teaching about the Spirit' instead. The word can confuse listeners who think it means the study of air or gases, so define it when speaking to general audiences.

distinctions.note: Pneumatics is physics or engineering dealing with gases and compressed air, while pneumatology is theology about the Holy Spirit.
Christology studies the person and work of Christ, while pneumatology studies the person and work of the Holy Spirit.

examples.everyday: At church last week, the speaker talked about pneumatology, and I had to ask what he meant by the Holy Spirit.
examples.professional: For the seminar paper, I am comparing two pneumatology chapters from different systematic theology textbooks.
examples.analytical: A robust pneumatology must account for both the Spirit's work in individual conversion and in the common life of the church.

nuance.analogy: Pneumatology is like the study of wind: you cannot see the Spirit directly, but you can trace its effects in the lives it moves.
nuance.etymology: From Greek pneuma (spirit, breath) and -logia (study of).
common_mistakes: Confusing pneumatology with pneumatics, the study of compressed air.
Stressing the wrong syllable as in 'nyoo-MAT-ol-oh-jee'.

senses.definition: A feature pertaining to the dynamic treatment of data elements based on their type, allowing for a method to have several definitions.
The ability to assume different forms or shapes.

The property of certain typed formal systems of allowing for the use of type variables and binders/quantifiers over those type variables; likewise, the property of certain expressions (within such typed formal systems) of making use of at least one such typed variable.
The ability of a solid material to exist in more than one form or crystal structure; pleomorphism.
The regular existence of two or more different genotypes within a given species or population; also, variability of amino acid sequences within a gene's protein.
The coexistence, in the same locality, of two or more distinct forms independent of sex, not connected by intermediate gradations, but produced from common parents.

core.definition: In software, the ability of one interface or method to work with different data types; in biology, the existence of several forms in one population.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'mor', the third syllable. The final syllable is a weak schwa, so say 'uhm', not 'izm' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in computing and biology.
nuance.usage_note: Programmers in American companies talk about polymorphism in object-oriented design, often in interviews and code reviews. Biologists use it for genetic variation within a species. Casual speakers would not use it and would describe something as 'having many forms' instead.

distinctions.note: Inheritance lets a class reuse another class's code, while polymorphism lets different classes respond to the same method call in their own way.
Overloading is a compile-time choice of method by parameter list, while polymorphism usually involves dynamic dispatch at runtime.

examples.everyday: My cousin is studying computer science, and she said polymorphism is the reason one button can do different things.
examples.professional: During the design review, we used polymorphism so that each payment provider implements the same charge method.
examples.analytical: Parametric polymorphism allows a single definition to operate uniformly over many types, which raises questions about the limits of abstraction.

nuance.analogy: Polymorphism is like a single job title, such as driver, that can be filled by a bus driver or a taxi driver, each doing the work in their own way.
nuance.etymology: From Greek polymorphos, having many forms, with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Saying 'polymorfism' with an f instead of a ph sound
Using polymorphism to mean overloading, which is a related but different concept

senses.definition: To give a sermon.
senses.example: Our pastor can preach very well.

senses.definition: To proclaim by public discourse; to utter in a sermon or a formal religious harangue.
To advise or recommend earnestly.
To teach or instruct by preaching; to inform by preaching.
To give advice in an offensive or obtrusive manner.
Used to express strong agreement (as if encouraging somebody to continue speaking).
senses.example: – If you can't do the time, don't do the crime! – Preach!

core.definition: To deliver a religious talk or sermon, usually based on a passage from Scripture, or to strongly urge a belief or behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Say the long 'ee' vowel clearly and end with a 'ch' sound. Make the 'r' strong at the start, as in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in church settings; negative when someone is lecturing others on unwanted advice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use preach for pastors and ministers in church, and for people who speak in a sermonizing way. Saying someone is 'preaching' at you means they are lecturing you, usually in an annoying way. In Black churches, the exclamation 'Preach!' or 'Preach it!' expresses strong agreement with a speaker, a usage found in everyday American speech too.

distinctions.note: Preaching aims to proclaim and persuade with religious authority; teaching aims to explain and inform.
A lecture is a formal talk, often academic; to preach suggests moral or religious urgency and can imply a sermon-like tone.

examples.everyday: My brother is always preaching about eating less sugar, even when I just want a donut.
examples.professional: Please don't preach the process at the team; show them the dashboard and let them decide.
examples.analytical: Paul's letters often preach the gospel by moving from the reality of grace to the demands of faithful living.

nuance.analogy: Preaching is like a bell ringing in a village square: it calls people to listen to a message they are meant to hear and act on.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praedicare, meaning to proclaim publicly.
common_mistakes: Confusing preach with 'teach' when describing a church talk.
Using preach as a noun, as in 'the preach was long'; the noun is sermon or preaching.
nuance.biblical_note: Greek kerussein (to proclaim as a herald) and euangelizesthai (to bring good news). Matthew 4:23 says Jesus went about teaching and preaching the gospel of the kingdom. Romans 10:14-15 asks how people can hear without a preacher. 1 Corinthians 1:21 speaks of God saving believers through the foolishness of what is preached.

traditions.view: Preaching, or homily, is central to worship and is grounded in the Scriptures and the teachings of the Fathers. The homily explains the faith in the context of the liturgy.
Preaching is an essential part of the Mass and the ministry of the priest and deacon, based on Scripture and Church tradition. The homily applies the readings to the faith life of the congregation.

Preaching of the Word is considered the central mark of the true Church, expounding Scripture to convict and build up believers. Forms vary from expository and topical to charismatic styles across denominations.

preach.etymology: From Middle English *prechen*, from Old French *prëechier*, *precchier*, from Latin *praedicō* (“to proclaim, announce”).

senses.definition: The condition of being precise; precision.
Pedantic behavior.

core.definition: The quality of being exact and carefully defined, with no vagueness or error.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SIGHS, the second syllable. The 'cise' sounds like 'sahys' with a long i, and the final 'ness' is a reduced 'nus'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, but it can sound fussy if the speaker means pedantic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say precision for this idea and use preciseness mostly in writing or to describe a person's careful habits. Preciseness can slightly suggest fussiness, so attention to detail is a warmer way to praise someone at work. The sense of pedantry is less common.

distinctions.note: Precision is the usual American word for exactness in measurement or work, while preciseness is less common and can sound more personal or fussy.
Accuracy means closeness to the true value, while preciseness describes how finely something is specified, even if it could be wrong.

examples.everyday: I appreciate her preciseness, since she always tells me exactly what time to meet.
examples.professional: The contract's preciseness about deadlines saved us from an argument later.
examples.analytical: The preciseness of Aristotle's definitions made his logic a model for generations of scholars.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-cut key that fits the lock exactly, with no wiggle.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praecisus, 'cut off, defined', plus the English suffix '-ness'.
common_mistakes: Using preciseness in technical talk, where precision is the usual American word.
Confusing the adjective precise with the noun; the noun is preciseness or precision.

senses.definition: To cause someone to become annoyed or angry.
senses.example: Don't provoke the dog; it may try to bite you.

senses.definition: To bring about a reaction.

core.definition: To make someone angry or upset, or to deliberately cause a reaction, emotion or event.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable VOHK. The final k is a clear, unreleased sound, and the vowel is the American oh, a long o with no glide.

nuance.connotation: Negative when it means to anger someone; neutral when it means to cause a reaction, such as provoke a discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say provoke in both everyday and formal speech. In casual talk, people more often say set someone off, push someone's buttons or get on someone's nerves. Provoke is common in news and writing, for example a question that provoked debate. It sounds strong, so it implies a deliberate or significant reaction.

distinctions.note: Irritate is milder and describes a feeling of annoyance, while provoke implies a stronger reaction, possibly anger or action.
Incite means to urge someone toward violence or unlawful action, while provoke is broader and need not involve any call to action.

examples.everyday: Don't let him provoke you; he just likes to start arguments at family dinners.
examples.professional: Her proposal provoked a lot of pushback from the design team, but it got people talking.
examples.analytical: The poem deliberately provokes the reader to question the assumptions behind the traditional account of faith.

nuance.analogy: To provoke someone is like pulling the trigger on a spring: a small push releases a sudden, strong response.
nuance.etymology: From Latin provocare, to call forth or challenge, from pro-, forth, and vocare, to call.
common_mistakes: Using provoke with a preposition like to or into; it takes a direct object, as in provoke someone into anger.
Confusing it with provoke as a noun; provoke is only a verb, and the noun is provocation.

provoke.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *provoquer*, from Old French, from Latin *prōvocāre*.

senses.definition: The state of being pungent.
A foul odor.

core.definition: The quality of having a strong, sharp taste or smell that stings the nose or tongue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PUN. The middle syllables are reduced, so say juhn-see with a weak vowel, and the g sounds like the j in judge.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing flavor, such as the pungency of fresh ginger; it can be negative for an unpleasant smell.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pungency mostly in food writing, wine or cheese descriptions, and cooking discussions. In everyday talk they would more often say the spice or the smell is strong. It is more common in print than in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Spiciness refers to heat, while pungency refers to a sharp, stinging quality of taste or smell that may not be hot.
Odor is a neutral word for any smell; pungency stresses that the smell is sharp and stinging.

examples.everyday: I love the pungency of fresh ginger in my tea, but my roommate says it's too strong.
examples.professional: The chef adjusted the pungency of the sauce so the herbs didn't overwhelm the fish.
examples.analytical: The essay traces how the pungency of early modern satire reflected a deliberate assault on polite manners.

nuance.analogy: Pungency is like a sharp voice in a quiet room; it grabs your attention right away.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pungens, pungent-, present participle of pungere, to prick or sting.
common_mistakes: Using pungency for a pleasant aroma; it usually suggests something sharp or stinging.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress is on PUN.

senses.definition: To assign a quantity to.
To determine the value of (a variable or expression).
To relate a statement (called a predicate) to a given set using a quantifier—either for all (denoted ∀) or there exists (denoted ∃).
senses.example: The statement (∀x∈ℝ)2x=x+x quantifies over the real numbers.

core.definition: To express or measure something as a number or amount.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KWAHN. The second syllable reduces to a quick schwa-like sound, and the final -fy rhymes with my.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes turning something into a number, which can be useful or reductive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use quantify in business, science and academic writing when turning a quality into a number. In casual talk, people say 'put a number on it' or 'figure out how much.' A natural reply is 'Can we measure that?'

distinctions.note: Measure is the everyday word for finding an amount; quantify stresses turning something less obviously measurable into a number.
Count applies to things you can enumerate; quantify also covers qualities and abstract factors.

examples.everyday: It's hard to quantify how much better I sleep since I started walking after dinner.
examples.professional: Can we quantify the impact of the new checkout flow on conversion before the review?
examples.analytical: Some philosophers insist that moral goods cannot be quantified without distorting what makes them good.

nuance.analogy: Like putting a price tag on a hug: possible, but it changes what is being valued.
nuance.etymology: From quantity, from Latin quantitas, 'how much', plus the verb suffix -fy.
common_mistakes: Using quantify as an adjective; the adjectives are quantifiable and quantitative.
Stressing the second syllable; say KWAHN-tih-fy.

senses.definition: The essence or inherent nature of a person or thing.
A trifle; a nicety or quibble.
An eccentricity; an odd feature.

core.definition: The essential nature or inherent character of a thing, the qualities that make it what it is.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second vowel is reduced to a short 'ih'. The final 'ty' is pronounced 'tee', not 'ti-ay'.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'quiddity' in philosophy, literary criticism or sophisticated writing, rarely in conversation. It is the sort of word a professor or essayist might use to describe what makes a person or idea distinctive. In everyday speech, people say 'essence' or 'nature' instead.

distinctions.note: Essence is the common word for the core nature of something; quiddity is more technical and philosophical, from scholastic terminology.
Nature is everyday and broad; quiddity focuses on the individual defining qualities of a particular thing.

collocations: the quiddity of the author's style

examples.everyday: That diner has a quiddity you don't find in chain restaurants, with its old booths and handwritten menus.
examples.professional: Our brand guidelines should capture the quiddity of the product, not just a list of its features.
examples.analytical: Aquinas distinguishes between a thing's existence and its quiddity, the what-it-is that answers the question of its essence.

nuance.analogy: Quiddity is like the fingerprint of a thing: the particular pattern that makes it itself and no other.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin quidditas, from Latin quid, 'what', literally 'whatness'.
common_mistakes: Using it in casual conversation where 'essence' or 'nature' would sound more natural.
Confusing it with 'quiddity' meaning a trifle, a rare older sense that is rarely used now.

quiddity.etymology: From Middle English *quidite*, from Old French *quidité*, and its source, Late Latin *quidditās*, from Latin *quid* (“what”) + *-itas* (“-ness”) (whence *-ity*).

senses.definition: Occurring on a quotidian basis; daily or commonplace.

core.definition: Every day, in a routine or commonplace way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, TID. The "-ian" ending is reduced to "un," and the final "-ly" is a clear, short "lee."

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes something routine without strong emotional coloring.
nuance.usage_note: This adverb is rare even in American writing and is most often found in essays or literary descriptions. In everyday speech, Americans would say "every day" or "daily" instead. Use it only when you want a formal, precise tone in writing.

distinctions.note: Daily is the normal everyday adverb; quotidianly is rarer and more literary.

examples.everyday: We walk the dog quotidianly, so it is hard to say we are doing anything special.
examples.professional: Our support team handles these tickets quotidianly, so the process needs to be simple and repeatable.
examples.analytical: The ritual was performed quotidianly, and its meaning lay precisely in its ordinariness.

nuance.analogy: If daily is a plain brown suitcase, quotidianly is the same bag described in a fancier catalog.
nuance.etymology: From quotidian, from Latin quotidianus, "daily."
common_mistakes: Using quotidianly in casual speech where "every day" sounds more natural.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the middle one.

senses.definition: The number resulting from the division of one number by another.
senses.example: Dividing 12 by 4 yields a quotient of 3.

senses.definition: By analogy, the result of any process that is the inverse of multiplication as defined for any mathematical entities other than numbers.
A mathematical structure formed by identifying elements within a larger one.
The number of runs scored per wicket lost when batting, divided by the number of runs conceded per wicket taken when bowling — used as a league table tiebreaker in some first-class tournaments.
To identify elements within a mathematical structure so as to create a quotient.

core.definition: The number that results when one number is divided by another.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, KWOH. The "-ent" ending is a reduced, unstressed "unt," not a full "ent."

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise; it is a technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use quotient almost entirely in math, statistics, and science classes or in discussions of measures such as IQ. In everyday speech it appears in phrases like "intelligence quotient" or "emotional quotient." Outside of those, people usually say "result" or "answer" of a division.

distinctions.note: A ratio compares two quantities, while a quotient is the result of dividing one number by another.
The remainder is what is left over after integer division; the quotient is the whole-number or main result.

examples.everyday: My daughter's math homework asked for the quotient of 84 divided by 7, and she got it right.
examples.professional: We report the cost per user as a quotient of total spend divided by active accounts, so the number is comparable across regions.
examples.analytical: In the quotient space, we identify points that differ by a symmetry, so the structure reflects the equivalence classes rather than the original points.

nuance.analogy: A quotient is like splitting a pizza evenly among friends: the number each person gets is the result of the division.
nuance.etymology: From Latin quotiens, "how many times," from quot, "how many."
common_mistakes: Confusing quotient with quota, which is a fixed share or limit.
Using quotient as the word for the whole division problem instead of the result.

senses.definition: A dried grape.
Of fruit: to dry out; to become like raisins.
To flavor (an alcoholic beverage) with fruit that has raisined.
To add raisins to.
To distribute throughout (with small bits or things), to dot or pepper.
To shrivel.
To crush or drain, so that all plumpness and vitality is gone.
To cause to have wrinkles.
To form wrinkles; to become wrinkled.

core.definition: A small, dried grape, dark and wrinkled, often eaten in cereal, baked goods, or trail mix.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is reduced to a weak 'un' sound (schwa plus n), not 'seen' or 'zeen.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral, and usually pleasant in food contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'raisin' constantly for dried grapes in cooking, breakfast cereal, and snacks, such as oatmeal raisin cookies. A dried grape is called a raisin only when it is dried, and the word is often used in food-shopping and recipe talk.

distinctions.note: Currants are a different, much smaller fruit (often from a different plant), and dried currants are used in British-style baking.
A sultana is a light, golden raisin made from a specific grape variety, sold more often in Britain than in the US.

examples.everyday: Can you grab a box of raisins at the store? I want to make oatmeal cookies.
examples.professional: The catering order needs raisins in the granola, so please check the allergen sheet.
examples.analytical: The Hebrew term for raisin cakes appears in the Samuel narratives as a gift of food for travelers.

nuance.analogy: A raisin is a grape that has spent its life in the sun and become concentrated and sweet.
nuance.etymology: From Old French raisin, 'grape,' from Latin racemus, 'cluster of grapes.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'rah-ZEEN' with stress on the second syllable.
Using 'raisin' for any dried fruit; raisins are specifically dried grapes.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, raisins (Hebrew tsimmuqim, 'raisin cakes' or pressed dried grape clusters) are a common food gift and provision. 1 Samuel 25:18 describes Abigail bringing raisins among her gifts to David. 1 Samuel 30:12 mentions an Egyptian servant revived with a cake of figs and two clusters of raisins. 2 Samuel 16:1 records Ziba bringing raisins to David as supplies.

raisin.etymology: From Middle English *raysyn*, borrowed from Anglo-Norman *raisin* (“grape, raisin”), from Late Latin *racīmus*, from Latin *racēmus*.

senses.definition: A defensive mound of earth or a wall with a broad top and usually a stone parapet; a wall-like ridge of earth, stones or debris; an embankment for defensive purpose.
A defensive structure; a protective barrier; a bulwark.
That which defends against intrusion from outside; a protection.
A steep bank of a river or gorge.
To defend with a rampart; fortify or surround with a rampart.

core.definition: A defensive wall or raised bank of earth, often with a walkway on top, built to protect a fort or city.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable has the cot vowel, pronounced like 'ah' in 'father', followed by a clear American r and a final t.

nuance.connotation: neutral to positive. It describes protection, though it can be used figuratively for a strong defense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use rampart in history, military writing, or literary and figurative speech. In everyday talk, people would more often say wall or fortification. In a figurative sense, it can describe a strong protection, as in ramparts of a legal argument.

distinctions.note: A wall is usually a vertical structure, while a rampart is typically a broad earthwork or a wall with a walkway along its top.
Bulwark is a near-synonym that is more often used figuratively for a defender of an idea, while rampart is more often physical.

examples.everyday: We walked along the old castle ramparts and looked out over the river.
examples.professional: The consultant described the firewall as the last rampart protecting our internal network.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have long treated certain intuitions as ramparts against skeptical arguments, though their defensive value is often overstated.

nuance.analogy: A rampart is like a long, stone-topped levee built to keep an enemy out rather than water.
nuance.etymology: From French rempart, from remparer, 'to fortify'.
common_mistakes: Confusing rampart with rampant, which means spreading out of control.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'pert' instead of the r-colored 'pahrt'.

rampart.etymology: Middle French *rempart* (“rampart of a fort”), from Old French *remparer* (“to defend, fortify, inclose with a rampart”), from *re-* + *emparer*, from Old Occitan *amparer*, from Vulgar Latin **anteparō* (“to prepare”), from *ante-* + *parō*.

senses.definition: A feeling of long-lasting ire for another, sometimes to the point of hatred, over a perceived wrongdoing; bitterness.
senses.example: I could almost see the rancor in his eyes when he challenged me to a fight.

senses.definition: Rancidity, rankness.

core.definition: Deep, bitter resentment toward someone that lasts a long time, often over a real or perceived wrong.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, RANG. The ng is a single nasal sound followed by k, and the final syllable is a rhotic er sound, so say it with a clear American r.

nuance.connotation: negative. It describes bitterness that lingers, and it is usually used to criticize people or disputes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rancor in news, political writing, and formal speech about long-lasting hostility, such as in a divorce or a dispute. In everyday talk they usually say bitterness or resentment instead. The phrase without rancor is common and natural for describing a respectful disagreement.

distinctions.note: Resentment is a general feeling of being wronged, while rancor is a stronger, longer-lasting bitterness.
A grudge is a specific reason to hold a grievance against someone, while rancor describes the general bitter feeling.

examples.everyday: There's no rancor left between my brother and me, even after that argument years ago.
examples.professional: The board debated the budget at length, but the members disagreed without rancor.
examples.analytical: Rancor often outlives its cause, hardening into an identity that the aggrieved person cannot easily abandon.

nuance.analogy: Rancor is like an old wound that keeps reopening because no one tends it properly.
nuance.etymology: From Latin rancor, 'rankness' or 'bitterness', from rancere, 'to stink', the same root as rancid.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling rancor in American writing.
Pronouncing it as RAN-ker, which drops the ng sound before k.

rancor.etymology: First attested in the 13th century as Middle English *rancour*, from Old French *rancor*, from Latin *rancor* (“rancidity, grudge, rancor”), from *ranceō* (“to be rotten or putrid”), from which also.

senses.definition: The dimensionality of an array or tensor.
The maximal number of linearly independent columns (or rows) of a matrix.
The maximum quantity of D-linearly independent elements of a module (over an integral domain D).
The size of any basis of a given matroid.
A row of people or things organized in a grid pattern, often soldiers.
senses.example: The front rank kneeled to reload while the second rank fired over their heads.

senses.definition: The value of a playing card.
senses.example: The ranks are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, Jack, Queen, King, and Ace.

senses.definition: One's position in a list sorted by a shared property such as physical location, population, popularity, or quality.
senses.example: Based on your test scores, you have a rank of 23.

senses.definition: The level of one's position in a class-based society.
A category of people, such as those who share an occupation or belong to an organization.
senses.example: a membership drawn from the ranks of wealthy European businessmen

senses.definition: A hierarchical level in an organization such as the military.
senses.example: Private First Class (PFC) is the second-lowest rank in the Marines.

senses.definition: A level in a scientific taxonomy system.
senses.example: Phylum is the taxonomic rank below kingdom and above class.

senses.definition: One of the eight horizontal lines of squares on a chessboard (i.e. those identified by a number).
In a pipe organ, a set of pipes of a certain quality for which each pipe corresponds to one key or pedal.
Strong in growth; growing with vigor or rapidity, hence, coarse or gross.
senses.example: rank grass

senses.definition: Causing strong growth; producing luxuriantly; rich and fertile.
senses.example: rank land

senses.definition: Suffering from overgrowth or hypertrophy; plethoric.
Strong to the senses; offensive; noisome.
Gross, disgusting, foul.
Headstrong; difficult to control.
Having a very strong, bad taste or odor.
senses.example: Your gym clothes are rank, bro – when'd you last wash 'em?

senses.definition: Complete, unmitigated, utter.
senses.example: rank treason

senses.definition: To place abreast or in a line.
To have a ranking.
senses.example: Their defense ranked third in the league.

senses.definition: To assign a suitable place in a class or order; to classify.
To take the rank of; to outrank.

core.definition: In linear algebra, the maximum number of linearly independent columns, or rows, of a matrix.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable, which ends in a distinct ng plus k blend. Do not drop the final k, and do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in mathematics.
nuance.usage_note: In American mathematics courses, rank is the standard term for this idea, and professors say the rank of the matrix. Outside technical work, rank usually means a position in an organization or a level of quality. The verb and adjective senses in this entry are old or literary and not typical in everyday American speech.

distinctions.note: Dimension is the size of a vector space; rank is the dimension of the space spanned by a matrix's columns or rows.
Nullity counts the dimension of the null space; rank plus nullity equals the number of columns.

examples.everyday: My friend in engineering said the rank of a matrix tells you how much real information it holds.
examples.professional: The model is unstable because the design matrix is not full rank, so we need to drop a redundant feature.
examples.analytical: Proving that the rank of a product is bounded by the smaller of the two ranks requires careful use of linear maps.

nuance.analogy: Rank is like the number of truly different directions in a crowd of arrows; many arrows may point the same way.
nuance.etymology: From Old French ranc, meaning row or line, from Germanic roots related to ring and rank.
common_mistakes: Confusing rank with dimension, which are related but not identical ideas
Using rank as a verb in technical math writing, which is not standard

rank.etymology: From Middle English *rank* (“strong, proud”), from Old English *ranc* (“proud, haughty, arrogant, insolent, forward, overbearing, showy, ostentatious, splendid, bold, valiant, noble, brave, strong, full-grown, mature”), from **rank*, from Proto-Germanic…

senses.definition: To calibrate for a second or subsequent time.

core.definition: To adjust a measuring instrument, model, or plan again so that it gives accurate results or meets new goals.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on KAL, the second syllable, and the 'a' in the first -a- syllable is reduced to 'uh'. The re- prefix is a quick 'ree' sound, and the final -ate is a clear 'ayt'.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it describes a technical or strategic adjustment without blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use recalibrate in engineering, science, data work, and business, for instance 'recalibrate the sensors' or 'recalibrate our expectations'. In a meeting it often means adjusting goals after new information. It is professional but not stiff, and it's common in everyday talk about adjusting plans.

distinctions.note: Calibrate means to set up an instrument for the first time or check it against a standard; recalibrate means doing it again.
Adjust is a general word for any small change; recalibrate implies a careful, systematic correction against a standard or a new reference point.
Reset means returning to a starting state; recalibrate means fine-tuning to restore accuracy.

examples.everyday: The kitchen scale was reading wrong, so I recalibrated it before weighing the flour.
examples.professional: After the new data came in, we recalibrated the forecasting model and cut the error rate in half.
examples.analytical: The author argues that reformers must recalibrate their metrics whenever the underlying social conditions shift.

nuance.analogy: Recalibrating is like tuning a guitar again after it has drifted out of pitch, so every string once again matches the standard.
nuance.etymology: From re- 'again' plus calibrate, from Latin calibrare, 'to fit to a standard', from Latin calibr-, 'a mold'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable, as in REE-kal-uh-brayt; the stress is on KAL.
Using it for a one-time setup; recalibrate implies doing it a second or later time.

senses.definition: An act or instance of reconnoitering.
senses.example: The pilot reported the findings of his reconnoiter.

senses.definition: To perform a reconnaissance (of an area; an enemy position); to scout with the aim of acquiring information.
senses.example: Our scout will reconnoiter the path ahead of our troops.

core.definition: To scout or survey an area or enemy position in order to gather information before taking action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, NOY, which rhymes with 'toy'; the last syllable is an American r-colored schwa, so it sounds like 'tur.' The American spelling is reconnoiter, and the first vowel is usually 'ee' in US speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it suggests careful, quiet exploration for information.
